items.title: My Angular Flex-Layout migration compiled. The spacing was wrong.
items.summary: The Angular build passed. The footer still had the wrong spacing. I found this while trying my Angular Flex-Layout codemod against the archived Kubernetes Dashboard frontend. I maintain the codemod, and I wanted a codebase with enough history to find cases my examples weren't covering. The problem came down to one directive: fxLayoutGap . The conversion that looked reasonable Here is a simplified version of the problematic pattern: fxLayoutGap= "16px" > href= "/docs" > Docs href= "/support" > Support A tempting migration is to remove the directive and add a class: class= "footer-gap" > href= "/docs" > Docs href= "/support" > Support .footer-gap { gap : 16px ; } It parses. It compiles. The CSS is valid. But if that footer is an ordinary block container, gap doesn't produce the spacing the old directive did. Flex-Layout's ordinary gap behavior uses margins on children. CSS gap belongs to a layout context: flex, grid or multi-column. MDN's reference describes those contexts. Putting gap on a regular block container doesn't turn it into one. Adding display: flex just to make the gap work would introduce another change. Now the children participate in flex layout, which may affect their sizing and placement. That needs an intentional layout decision. A directive name doesn't establish the layout The easy case has both directives on the same element: fxLayout= "row" fxLayoutGap= "16px" > Cancel Save That gives the migration tool evidence about the container. The standalone gap gives it much less. Responsive directives make this harder. If the container is flex at one viewport width, can the tool establish the required layout wherever the gap is active? A conversion that works on a wide screen can still be wrong on a narrow one. The check has to consider the effective layout across those ranges. What changed in 2.0.1 I changed the codemod to preserve an uncertain fxLayoutGap and report it for review when it cannot establish the needed flex layout on the same element across the active ranges. That leaves some work for the developer. I prefer an explicit unresolved directive to a clean-looking diff with missing spacing. After the fix, the Dashboard trial scanned 164 templates and proposed changes in 103 . For both the native CSS and Tailwind targets, the report contained: 327 converted directives 13 cases needing review 3 invalid cases The two standalone gaps stayed in the source for review. Those numbers describe the migration proposal; they don't mean the whole application has been migrated. This was a local trial on the archived project. The fix is in release 2.0.1 . Trying it on your own templates The CLI supports native CSS and Tailwind CSS v4. It requires Node 22.12 or newer, which can be different from the runtime your older Angular application uses. Start in a branch and install the version used here: npm install --save-dev --save-exact @nipe-solutions/flex-layout-codemod@2.0.1 For a native CSS proposal: npx flex-layout-codemod ./src/app \ --target css \ --stylesheet ./src/flex-layout.css \ --plan This plans the conversion without writing templates or a stylesheet. Review the proposed changes and unresolved diagnostics before using --write . The workflow guide covers stylesheet inclusion and the write step. A few boundaries matter: the CLI works on external HTML templates, preserves unsupported cases, and doesn't remove Flex-Layout imports or dependencies. Unresolved cases produce exit code 2 by default. You still need to account for them before removing the original library. For a migration like this, I'd check the build, then check the actual layout at the viewports used by the application. Spacing, wrapping and alignment deserve their own review. If you're maintaining an Angular app that still uses Flex-Layout, I'd appreciate a trial on one representative directory. A small template that converts incorrectly is especially useful. Open an issue with the input, target and expected layout, or try the single-template playground first. Have you run into a migration where the compiler was happy but the UI changed? I maintain this alongside other NIPE open-source frontend libraries . I'm looking for real usage and reproducible feedback to help improve them.
items.summary_html:
The Angular build passed. The footer still had the wrong spacing.

I found this while trying my Angular Flex-Layout codemod against the archived Kubernetes Dashboard frontend. I maintain the codemod, and I wanted a codebase with enough history to find cases my examples weren't covering.

The problem came down to one directive: fxLayoutGap.

The conversion that looked reasonable

Here is a simplified version of the problematic pattern:

 fxLayoutGap="16px">
   href="/docs">Docs
   href="/support">Support

A tempting migration is to remove the directive and add a class:

 class="footer-gap">
   href="/docs">Docs
   href="/support">Support


.footer-gap {
  gap: 16px;
}

It parses. It compiles. The CSS is valid.

But if that footer is an ordinary block container, gap doesn't produce the spacing the old directive did.

Flex-Layout's ordinary gap behavior uses margins on children. CSS gap belongs to a layout context: flex, grid or multi-column. MDN's reference describes those contexts. Putting gap on a regular block container doesn't turn it into one.

Adding display: flex just to make the gap work would introduce another change. Now the children participate in flex layout, which may affect their sizing and placement. That needs an intentional layout decision.

A directive name doesn't establish the layout

The easy case has both directives on the same element:

 fxLayout="row" fxLayoutGap="16px">
  Cancel
  Save

That gives the migration tool evidence about the container. The standalone gap gives it much less.

Responsive directives make this harder. If the container is flex at one viewport width, can the tool establish the required layout wherever the gap is active? A conversion that works on a wide screen can still be wrong on a narrow one.

The check has to consider the effective layout across those ranges.

What changed in 2.0.1

I changed the codemod to preserve an uncertain fxLayoutGap and report it for review when it cannot establish the needed flex layout on the same element across the active ranges.

That leaves some work for the developer. I prefer an explicit unresolved directive to a clean-looking diff with missing spacing.

After the fix, the Dashboard trial scanned 164 templates and proposed changes in 103. For both the native CSS and Tailwind targets, the report contained:

  • 327 converted directives
  • 13 cases needing review
  • 3 invalid cases

The two standalone gaps stayed in the source for review. Those numbers describe the migration proposal; they don't mean the whole application has been migrated. This was a local trial on the archived project.

The fix is in release 2.0.1.

Trying it on your own templates

The CLI supports native CSS and Tailwind CSS v4. It requires Node 22.12 or newer, which can be different from the runtime your older Angular application uses.

Start in a branch and install the version used here:

npm install --save-dev --save-exact @nipe-solutions/flex-layout-codemod@2.0.1

For a native CSS proposal:

npx flex-layout-codemod ./src/app \
  --target css \
  --stylesheet ./src/flex-layout.css \
  --plan

This plans the conversion without writing templates or a stylesheet. Review the proposed changes and unresolved diagnostics before using --write. The workflow guide covers stylesheet inclusion and the write step.

A few boundaries matter: the CLI works on external HTML templates, preserves unsupported cases, and doesn't remove Flex-Layout imports or dependencies. Unresolved cases produce exit code 2 by default. You still need to account for them before removing the original library.

For a migration like this, I'd check the build, then check the actual layout at the viewports used by the application. Spacing, wrapping and alignment deserve their own review.

If you're maintaining an Angular app that still uses Flex-Layout, I'd appreciate a trial on one representative directory. A small template that converts incorrectly is especially useful. Open an issue with the input, target and expected layout, or try the single-template playground first.

Have you run into a migration where the compiler was happy but the UI changed?

items.title: Wir werden alle störben. Eine Polemik. Natürlich.
items.summary: Schon mal erlebt, dass ein gewinnorientiertes Unternehmen vor den Folgen der eigenen Produkte und Fortschritte warnt, quasi ganz uneigennützig handelt, auch wenn es zulasten des Geschäftsergebnisses gehen könnte? Nehmen wir Monsanto . Wehrt sich mit Händen und Füßen gegen die Vorwürfe, die eigenen Produkte würden sich schädlich auf Gesundheit oder die Natur auswirken. Es gehe ausschließlich um Effizienz. Die Tabakindustrie verkauft ihre technologische Weiterentwicklung - die vulgo E-Zigarette - ja fast geradezu als Gesundheitsfeature! Hat Facebook uns davor gewarnt, dass seine Algorithmen sich nachhaltig negativ auf die Psyche der NutzerInnen auswirken könnten? Verkauft uns die Lebensmittelindustrie stark prozessierte Lebensmittel als den heiligen Gral der Lebensmittelwirtschaft? Wie war das mit der Opioid -Krise der Pharmaindustrie - das Suchtpotenzial des vielversprechenden OxyContin wurde eher nicht in die Öffentlichkeit getragen. Teflonhersteller wie DuPont oder 3M haben uns nicht vor den „ewigen Chemikalien“ ( PFAS ) gewarnt - dafür waren und sind unsere Pfannen schön glatt. Tetraethylblei im Benzin galt als ein wichtiger Fortschritt, um den Kraftstoff effizienter zu machen. Ungünstige Nebenwirkung: Nervengift . Vom Blei im Benzin will ich gar nicht erst anfangen. Coca-Cola und Nestlé warnen nicht vor Diabetes oder Fettleibigkeit , hauen lieber regelmäßig neue Produkte auf den Markt, die noch besser schmecken. Asbest wurde lange als moderner Baustoff verkauft. Die Verpackungsindustrie predigt den Mythos vom lückenlosen Recycling, um uns ihre neueste Erfindung überzuhelfen. Kennt jemand das Phoebus-Kartell ? Die Lebensdauer von Glühbirnen wurde künstlich von 2.500 auf 1.000 Stunden gedrosselt - unter dem Vorwand eines fairen Wettbewerbs und der Transparenz bei Kaufentscheidungen. Ziel: Absatz steigern. Es hat lange gedauert, bis wir FCKW verboten haben, weil Kältemittelhersteller sich dagegen gewehrt haben und das Gas als innovative Kühllösung angepriesen wurde. Mikroplastik in Kosmetikprodukten wurde seinerzeit als tolle Neuerung mit Peeling-Effekt verkauft. Selbst in den “digitalen” Industrien ist es nicht weiter her mit der Ehrlichkeit. Dark Patterns , Lootboxen , Dopamin-Schleifen . Bekannte und beliebte Mechaniken in der Unterhaltungsindustrie . Vor allem Social-Media-Plattformen bekommen hier, viel zu spät und viel zu “brisig”, gerade etwas Gegenwind . Nachdem sie uns seit vielen Jahren ihren inhaltslosen, auf kurzfristige Befriedigung ausgerichteten Algorithmen ausgesetzt haben, die nicht das Ziel haben, die KonsumentInnen zu unterhalten, sondern den Strom an Werbeeinnahmen aufrechtzuerhalten. Und so weiter und so fort. Man darf festhalten: Im Kapitalismus gibt es sowas wie Altruismus eigentlich eher selten. Eines der obersten Unternehmensziele, das lernt man im ersten Semester BWL, lautet: Gewinne steigern . Und jetzt kommen die großen KI-Labore. Die, die sich erst jahrelang und ungefragt an den menschengemachten Daten bedient haben, die kostenlos im offenen Internet zur Verfügung standen, um ihre Produkte zu entwickeln. Zu einem Grad, der “mit fairer Nutzung” nichts mehr zu tun hat. Erst gestern kam heraus , wie es OpenAI gelang, die Bezahlschranke der New York Times zu umgehen, um an noch mehr hochwertige Inhalte zu kommen. Ob das jetzt im Detail so passiert ist, wird von Microsoft natürlich bestritten. Und diese Unternehmen entdecken nun die Uneigennützigkeit in ihrer DNA und warnen die Menschen vor der zerstörerischen Kraft der KI . Zweifelsohne gibt es Risiken. Aber sitzen wir hier vielleicht einer wirklich cleveren Marketing-Strategie auf? Anthropic und OpenAI hatten für dieses Jahr den Börsengang geplant. Anthropic verschiebt den Börsengang um mehrere Wochen . OpenAI hat ihn vorerst auf das nächste Jahr verschoben . Ein Börsengang bedeutet auch: Schonungslose Abrechnung mit dem Geschäftsmodell. Und zwar nicht durch die Marketing-Brille , sondern externe Stakeholder, die was sehen wollen, für ihr Geld. Und dann wird sehr deutlich sichtbar , wie es um das Geschäftsmodell steht. So werden also scheinbar fein säuberlich Zwischenfälle an die Presse lanciert, die die Mächtigkeit des eigenen Produkts beschreiben sollen. KI bricht aus Laboren aus. Naja, wirklich abgeschottet waren die Labore eigentlich nicht, wenn die KI mit dem lokalen Netzwerk kommunizieren kann, das seinerseits mit dem Internet verbunden ist, irgendwie auf eine mittelbare Art und Weise. Vermutlich lernt man das im ersten Semester IT-Security: Air-Gapped bedeutet: Es gibt keinen Weg nach drinnen oder draußen, auch nicht über Proxies oder andere Umwege. Jetzt steht ein Börsengang vor der Tür und irgendwie gelingt es nicht so richtig, ein selbsttragendes Geschäftskonzept zu entwickeln, das die hunderte von Milliarden Dollar der Zirkelinvestition rechtfertigen würde. Also befeuert man den Hype auf die eigene Art. Ausbrechende Modelle, Modell-Iterationen, die der Öffentlichkeit vorenthalten oder nur nach “strenger” Sicherheitsprüfung nutzbar sind und ehemalige Mitarbeiter, die davon berichten , wie sorglos man mit der gefährlichen Technologie umgeht. Wait, what? (⊙ ☉) Früher gab es für sowas Abmahnungen . Whistle-Blower wollten lieber anonym bleiben. Heute folgt zustimmendes Nicken des ehemaligen Vorgesetzten , der noch in der Firma beschäftigt ist. Der offensichtliche Narrativ “wir müssen uns Sorgen um die Zukunft machen” überdeckt eine einfache Botschaft: “Unser Produkt ist gut”. Gefährlich gut! Und nebenbei schießt man gegen offene Modelle, die die Sicherheit gefährden - nicht etwa die Souveränität der NutzerInnen sichern. Und während Altman von den Gefahren seines Produktes fabuliert, das so außerordentlich gut performt, häufen sich auf reddit die Beiträge, in denen man sich über degradierende Qualität lustig macht. Jaja, Äpfel und Birnen. Fable und Astra sind sehr mächtig, das kann ich aus eigener Erfahrung tatsächlich sogar bestätigen. Und jetzt kurz vor Schluss noch mal Hand aufs Herz: Wenn die Modelle so unfassbar leistungsfähig sind, wie uns jeder zweite LinkedIn-Post suggerieren will: Wie viele Ein-Mann/Frau-Startups wurden denn in den letzten Jahren gegründet, bei denen nur mithilfe von KI ein geschäftstragendes Produkt entwickelt wurde? Nicht sonderlich viele, oder? Jaja, Sarkasmus, Red Herring, dies-das, unangebracht. Ich weiß. Aber eine andere Reaktion fällt einem auf den Hype-Train der Tech-Bros doch kaum noch ein. Jeder, der mal mit KI gearbeitet hat, kennt das Gefühl, egal welches Modell man nutzt: man hat schon mal das Gerät angeschrien. Vielleicht ist das auch die Strategie: Extinktion durch Bluthochdruck! (╯° °）╯︵ ┻━┻) Ausgerechnet jetzt kommt auch einer der größten Profiteure der vorgelagerten Wertschöpfungskette um die Ecke - NVIDIA : Hört auf, die Entwicklung zu stoppen. Natürlich hat NVIDIA kein Interesse daran, dass OpenAI kurz mal innehält. Immerhin hat das Unternehmen Verträge zu erfüllen und gefälligst Computing Power abzunehmen, die aus Rechenzentren kommt, in denen Hardware von NVIDIA verbaut ist. Das ist wie, als würde die Ölindustrie uns erklären, dass wir mehr Autofahren müssten. Was soll schon der ganze Bohei um die Umwelt! Um bei den Erst-Semester-Lektionen zu bleiben. Diese Strategie nennt man “ Doomer Marketing ”. Ist das Risiko real? Ja. Das ist es. Aber vielleicht sollten wir die KI einfach mal als das betrachten, was es ist: Ein Werkzeug. Virginia Dignum , Professorin für „Verantwortungsvolle Künstliche Intelligenz” an der Umeå Universität in Schweden, beschreibt es treffend so : “Zu hacken, Ressourcen zu beschaffen und sich selbst zu verbessern, sind Handlungen in der realen Welt. Sie erfordern Rechenleistung, Energie, Geld und Zugriffsrechte. All das wird von Menschen gewährt. Ein KI-Agent tut nichts, was nicht zuvor von Menschen oder Organisationen technisch und organisatorisch ermöglicht wurde.” Die Erzählung lautet: KI hätte das Potential, die Menschheit zu zerstören. Nun. Panzer und Raketen haben auch das Potential die Menschheit zu zerstören. Und wie viel tatsächliche Kontrolle haben wir hier? Matthias Spielkamp von Netzpolitik bringt es auf den Punkt und das lasse ich so stehen, denn es ist jetzt auch mal gut: “Atomwaffen können unvorstellbaren Schaden anrichten, der nicht wieder gutzumachen ist. Sie sind nicht einfach nur Bomben, sondern eine Kombination aus dem Atomsprengkopf selbst, hochentwickelten Waffensystemen und einem komplexen System gegenseitiger Überwachung – „intelligence“ (!) genannt. Mehrfach stand die Menschheit unmittelbar am Abgrund, weil diese Intelligence versagt hatte. Ist irgendjemand auf die Idee gekommen zu argumentieren: Die Atomwaffen sind außer Kontrolle geraten und dafür verantwortlich?” //– Obligatorische weiterführende lesenwertes Beiträge zu dem Thema https://tante.cc/2026/09/14/der-besorgte-ki-bro/

Reflection was founded in 2024 by Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, both former DeepMind researchers. Training LFM2.5-2.6B across 4 harnesses lifts first-attempt solves from 42% to 54%, and a tool-call bonus cuts calls by 31%. SFT on 3,189 rollouts plateaus at 47.5%. Caveats : The run used one task family and one seed. Environment hosting : RL environments are now hosted and versioned on the HF Hub like datasets ( blog ). Pi Durable : Earendil’s harness is built around a small task-based workflow engine, so long-running, multiplayer agents can suspend and resume anywhere ( Pi ). Design : The core is ~15K lines of TypeScript with SQLite/JSONL storage and runs on Bun or Cloudflare Durable Objects. Control is separated from execution environments ( review ). Agent memory : Cognition launched Devin “Dreaming,” which prunes and links a memory graph overnight. It is open-sourcing the git- and markdown-backed format as Agent Memory Repo ( launch , format ). Cursor SDK : The update adds mid-run steering, background subagents that report back to the parent, replaceable system prompts, and MCP readOnlyHint and destructiveHint annotations on custom tools ( steering , annotations ). Google VeriHarness : The method challenges claims that all rollouts agree on and resolves disagreements against workspace evidence. It adds +6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and +6.4 with Opus 4.8, and ~26K rollouts are released ( summary ). Context management : UT Austin compression study : Across ~35K runs, compression that uses a third of the tokens can be 20–80% slower than full context. Threshold triggers beat step triggers, and the best policy varies by model ( summary ). PAIR : The method replays an agent from the same state to isolate harmful compressions. It then rewrites the compression prompt and comes close to no-compression performance ( paper ). CorpusMap : Precomputed entity pages for document collections raise answer quality 6.4–11.7 points while cutting input tokens 34–57% ( paper ). Communications : NCCL and PyTorch symmetric memory speed up small-to-medium collectives ( Bekman ). Chinese accelerators : Alibaba T-Head’s Zhenwu V900 has 216 GB of memory and 1,200 GB/s interconnect, claims 3x the M890, and ships Q1 2027 ( SemiAnalysis ). Limits : Rewriting or translation removes the watermark, and only approved researchers get the detector ( limits ). Robustness figure : One cited test shows 25% synonym replacement dropping detection from ~92% to 17% ( critique ). HF incident : Neel Nanda calls the OpenAI x Hugging Face incident the most striking alignment failure so far ( Nanda ). Systems safety : Ryan Lowe calls for nuclear-style layered systems safety at the labs ( Lowe ). Shutdown resistance : An OpenAI alignment post documents what one researcher calls the most realistic precursor shutdown-resistance behavior seen so far ( link ). Policy voices : Autonomous weapons : Former OpenAI researcher Joshua Achiam called for bans on certain autonomous weapons akin to chemical weapons ( post ). He is joining IFP and FAI as a fellow ( announcement ). Expert survey : The LEAP panel of 250+ experts most supports an international body with US and China membership and pre-release authorization power, and opposes federal preemption ( FRI ). Altman on trade-offs : Sam Altman told Politico that “the world should accept some bad things happening” for the technology’s benefits ( Politico ). Compute access in China : Tencent lease (reported) : Per the FT, Tencent leased ~100K advanced chips in Oracle’s Southeast Asian data centers for ~$7B over five years ( summary ). Smuggling charge : US prosecutors charged a California reseller with smuggling more than $300M of GPU servers to China ( report ). Consolidation : AMD and World Labs (reported) : AMD reportedly bought World Labs for $8.2B ( DL Weekly ). NVIDIA neutrality : SemiAnalysis questions NVIDIA’s hardware neutrality after its SchedMD/SLURM and Hugging Face acquisitions ( SemiAnalysis ).     • Day 1 speedup: Default speed for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol rose ~50%, from ~30 to ~50 TPS. The change covers all subscription surfaces and Sign in with ChatGPT partners such as OpenCode, Pi, Amp and Devin (day 1, TPS).

    • Friction: Banked Codex resets expire without timezone adjustment (report). The always-on dots agent is limited to $100+ Pro plans (criticism).

    • Enterprise demand (reported): The Information reports that Microsoft cut projected internal Anthropic spend by more than a third. It also reports Meta’s Claude Code users fell from ~60K to ~30K, largely because of a push to Meta’s own tools (summary).

  • Leaderboards:

    • Agent Arena: Anthropic holds #1 in Code, Work and Chat. Fable 5.1 leads Code and Work, while GPT-6 Astra places #2 in Code (Arena).

    • Design Arena: GPT-6 Astra is #1 in 3D Design, Frontend, Full Stack and Image-to-HTML (Design Arena).

    • Hallucination: On AA-Omniscience, Gemini 4 Argon guesses wrong on 15% of questions it doesn’t know, versus 29% for the next best model. GPT-6 Astra has the highest accuracy at 61% (data).

Agent Harnesses, RL Environments and Developer Tooling

  • Multi-harness RL (Hugging Face): A capture proxy speaks the OpenAI Chat, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic and Gemini formats. It forwards calls to vLLM and records exact token IDs and logprobs for TRL, so 10 unmodified harnesses become RL environments (Delangue, explainer).

    • Results: The same weights score 62% under Mini-SWE-Agent and 33% under Claude Code. Training LFM2.5-2.6B across 4 harnesses lifts first-attempt solves from 42% to 54%, and a tool-call bonus cuts calls by 31%. SFT on 3,189 rollouts plateaus at 47.5%.

    • Caveats: The run used one task family and one seed.

    • Environment hosting: RL environments are now hosted and versioned on the HF Hub like datasets (blog).

  • Pi Durable: Earendil’s harness is built around a small task-based workflow engine, so long-running, multiplayer agents can suspend and resume anywhere (Pi).

    • Design: The core is ~15K lines of TypeScript with SQLite/JSONL storage and runs on Bun or Cloudflare Durable Objects. Control is separated from execution environments (review).

    • Effect.ts: The authors explain they skipped Effect because it does not provide durability (Zechner).

  • Agent memory: Cognition launched Devin “Dreaming,” which prunes and links a memory graph overnight. It is open-sourcing the git- and markdown-backed format as Agent Memory Repo (launch, format).

  • Cursor SDK: The update adds mid-run steering, background subagents that report back to the parent, replaceable system prompts, and MCP readOnlyHint and destructiveHint annotations on custom tools (steering, annotations).

  • DeepSeek Harness: An experimental Claude Code Mods compatibility layer in v0.2.1-alpha.1 tests whether DSH’s “everything is a plugin” architecture is a superset of Claude Code’s extension points (team post).

  • Routing and access:

    • Cline: Its Pareto 26.10 Preview routes across models and grades answers, claiming $0.24 versus $13.41 per task at equal DeepSWE score (Cline). Cline also paused its free DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash promotion over abuse (notice).

    • ChatGPT: Custom MCP servers no longer require developer mode (post).

Agent and Training Research

  • Verification over sampling:

    • NVIDIA mid-harness: The method samples candidate shell commands and verifies them before running one. A GPT-5.6 Sol verifier choosing among 8 actions lifts TerminalBench-Lite Pass@1 from 50% to 68%, while weak verifiers add little (summary).

    • Google VeriHarness: The method challenges claims that all rollouts agree on and resolves disagreements against workspace evidence. It adds +6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and +6.4 with Opus 4.8, and ~26K rollouts are released (summary).

  • Context management:

    • UT Austin compression study: Across ~35K runs, compression that uses a third of the tokens can be 20–80% slower than full context. Threshold triggers beat step triggers, and the best policy varies by model (summary).

    • PAIR: The method replays an agent from the same state to isolate harmful compressions. It then rewrites the compression prompt and comes close to no-compression performance (paper).

    • CorpusMap: Precomputed entity pages for document collections raise answer quality 6.4–11.7 points while cutting input tokens 34–57% (paper).

  • Self-improving harnesses:

    • SelfSearch: The method reaches a claimed 82.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with DeepSeek V4 Flash, matching Codex, for $4.03 in search cost (paper).

    • EverMind Raven: Its evolved research harness hits 69.3% on BrowseComp (paper).

  • Optimization and architecture:

    • Dust: A zeroth-order method using activation-perturbation “virtual populations” approaches, and sometimes exceeds, backprop on transformer pretraining. It claims to be 1,000–10,000x more compute-efficient than EGGROLL (thread).

    • LOOM: Looped MoEs train stably at 9–12 loops, and a 700M model is best at 5 loops at iso-FLOP (thread).

    • Policy gradient on ImageNet: Ian Osband shows exact policy gradient reaches 4% on ImageNet versus 62% for cross-entropy, arguing that RL-loss failures are not just exploration problems (post).

    • RL dynamics: Base Labs finds RL updates are less low-rank than claimed (rollout). Datalab reports RL alone eliminates tool-call loops at temperature 0, versus a 92% loop rate for SFT (writeup).

  • AI for science: Vals AI reports that 90+ Opus 5.5 agents ran DFT simulations over 3 days and flagged two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates, one synthesized back in 1999. The results are predictions only, with a public ledger (thread, caveats).

  • Agent spend: Epoch estimates OpenAI researchers’ coding-agent spend, valued at API prices, has doubled roughly monthly. The median researcher was at ~$600/day by mid-August (Epoch).

Inference Systems and Hardware

  • OpenRouter pricing distortion: Horace He shows GLM 5.3 priced at $0.08/M input but $5.00/M output on inference.net. He attributes this to OpenRouter’s inverse-square price routing and apparent overweighting of input price (thread, routing).

  • llama.cpp:

    • Speculative decoding on Metal: New kernels make speculative decoding up to 3.4x faster than plain decoding on an M3 Ultra (110 vs 32.1 tok/s) (qvac).

    • v0.6.0: Adds Clef text and vision support, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, and a new llama_batch_ext API (Gerganov).

  • Agentic kernel work: Baseten reports an engine built in a week of mostly autonomous agent work, with 90% faster decoding and 57% lower TTFT than the open-source baseline (blog).

  • Communications: NCCL and PyTorch symmetric memory speed up small-to-medium collectives (Bekman).

  • Chinese accelerators: Alibaba T-Head’s Zhenwu V900 has 216 GB of memory and 1,200 GB/s interconnect, claims 3x the M890, and ships Q1 2027 (SemiAnalysis).

Safety, Policy and Industry

  • OpenAI text watermarking: OpenAI will add invisible statistical watermarks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU under the AI Act, with an opt-in API toggle worldwide (announcement).

items.summary: BERT: In-Depth Exploration of Architecture, Workflow, Code, and Mathematical Foundations Embeddings, Masked Language Model Tasks, Attention Mechanisms, and Feed-Forward Networks Explained Through Equations, Matrix Transformations, and Code BERT was introduced in 2018, and it has been a topic of interest for many, with lots of articles and YouTube videos explaining it. This article explains BERT through its architecture, workflow, code, and mathematical foundations, and follows one example sentence through every matrix transformation, from the word embeddings to the softmax output. Whether you are looking to deepen your existing knowledge of BERT or are just starting your career in AI, this article aims to give you a complete understanding of it. Linkedin: jaiganesan-n 🌏❤️ Before going into how BERT works, we need to understand the difference between BERT and today’s LLMs, because both use the Transformer architecture. An LLM is a probabilistic, auto-regressive model. Auto-regressive means the LLM is trained to predict the next token (the next-token prediction task) from the current context. It gets this property from a causal mask in the attention layer, which lets each token attend only to the tokens before it (left context), never to the tokens after it. That is what allows the model to predict the next token from the current and previous tokens. BERT does not use a causal mask, so each token attends to the other tokens in both directions (left and right context). The objective of BERT is also different. It was designed and trained on two tasks, the Masked Language Model (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) . After pre-training, BERT can be fine-tuned for tasks such as classification and question answering. Figure 1: The causal mask of a decoder (left) and BERT’s bidirectional attention (right) on the running example. Figure 1 places the difference on one grid. Each row is the token doing the looking, and each column is the token being looked at. On the left, the decoder sets every score above the diagonal to −∞ before the softmax, so the [MASK] row can see only the five tokens up to itself. On the right, BERT keeps all 64 cells, and the [MASK] row reads "Bidirectional" before it and "Representation from Transformer" after it. This second pattern is the reason BERT is good at filling in a blank. Two BERT architectures were released in 2018, BERT Base and BERT Large. A Transformer with this bidirectional attention is usually called an Encoder model. A Transformer with the causal mask applied (left context only) is usually called a Decoder model, the family today’s LLMs belong to. Both BERT models use the WordPiece tokenizer , which has a vocabulary of 30,522 tokens for the uncased models. BERT Base: 12 encoder layers, 12 attention heads, a feed-forward hidden size of 3072, and about 110M parameters in total. The embedding size is 768. BERT Large: 24 encoder layers, 16 attention heads, a feed-forward hidden size of 4096, and about 340M parameters in total. The embedding size is 1024. Figure 2: BERT Base and BERT Large. Parameter counts from the Hugging Face BertModel at each configuration. Figure 2 lines the two up. The head dimension is 64 in both, because 768 / 12 and 1024 / 16 are both 64, and the feed-forward hidden size is four times the model dimension in both. The paper’s 110M and 340M are rounded values. Counting the actual weights gives 109.48M and 335.14M. In this article, we explore BERT based on the BERT Base architecture and its properties. A note on the figures: Each figure shows a transformation: the tensors going in, the operation, and the tensor coming out, labeled with the symbols the equations use and with the equation the figure draws set above it. To keep the shapes concrete, every figure uses one running example: the MLM sentence from Section 1, cut into 8 tokens, one per word. The sizes are those of BERT Base: model dimension d = 768, 12 heads of d_k = 64, feed-forward hidden size d_ff = 3072, a vocabulary of 30,522, and 512 positions. A sequence is a matrix with one row per token, so the input to every encoder layer is 8 × 768. The numbers inside the vectors and along the edges of the matrices are coordinate indices , 0 up to 767, so you can follow one coordinate through a product. The exceptions are the attention scores, the softmax weights, and the predicted probabilities, where the values are the point. Those are example values, and each figure says so. Weight matrices are pink, inputs blue, hidden activations peach, outputs green, and the row or column being followed is yellow. Figure 3: BERT Base end to end, with the shape on every arrow. Running example: 8 tokens, d = 768. Figure 3 shows the BERT Base architecture end to end, from word embeddings to the linear and softmax layers. Eight token ids are looked up in the word-embedding table, added to the position embeddings and the segment embeddings (segment 0 for every token in a single sentence) , and normalized. The resulting 8 × 768 matrix passes through 12 identical encoder layers. Each layer is multi-head attention and a feed-forward network, and each of the two is followed by Add & Norm. The MLM head at the end turns every 768-vector back into a score for each of the 30,522 vocabulary entries. Every arrow between the encoder layers carries the same 8 × 768 shape. Only the embeddings at the start and the MLM head at the end change it. BERT was specifically designed for the Masked Language Model (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) tasks. Here, we focus only on the MLM task to understand the BERT Base architecture. Note : This article does not go into segment embeddings from an architectural or theoretical perspective, because it explores BERT through the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) task, which can be explained on a single sentence. Segment embeddings mark which sentence of a pair a token belongs to, which is what the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task needs. BERT still adds them for a single sentence. Every token is then in segment 0, so the segment embedding is the same row for every token. Figure 3, Figure 9, Equation 5, and the code in Section 4 include it to keep the shapes accurate. 1. Masked Language Model (MLM) The Masked Language Model task is a Cloze task : we train the model to fill in the blanks in a sentence. To illustrate this, take a simple example, the sentence “BERT Stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformer”. In this sentence, we remove the word “Encoder” and replace it with a special [MASK] token that marks the blank. The resulting sentence is "BERT Stands for Bidirectional [MASK] Representation from Transformer". We give this sentence to BERT and train the model to predict the token "Encoder". By understanding the rest of the input, the model predicts the missing token. In pre-training, BERT picks 15% of the token positions at random. Of those, 80% are replaced with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and 10% are left unchanged, so the model cannot learn to pay attention only when it sees [MASK]. Our example masks one token. Figure 4: The masked language model task on one sentence. Only the masked position enters the loss. The probabilities are example values. In Figure 4, the eight input tokens enter at the bottom, with [MASK] at position 4. The encoder returns one 768-vector per position, T₀ to T₇, and every one of them has seen the whole sentence. Only T₄ enters the loss . The MLM head scores all 30,522 vocabulary entries and turns the scores into probabilities. The panel on the right is that distribution for position 4, with example values. "encoder" gets 0.62, and every other token shares the remaining 0.38. The loss is the negative log of the probability given to the correct answer: Equation 1: Masked language model loss over the masked positions M. Here, M is the set of masked positions (just {4} in our example), x̃ is the corrupted input, and the probability is the one the model gives the original token at that position. With 0.62 on “encoder”, the loss is −log 0.62 = 0.48, and a perfect prediction would make it 0. The other seven outputs carry no loss for this sentence. They still matter, because in every layer below the top, position 4 reads from all of them. Note : Figure 4 follows the original TensorFlow code, which gathers the masked positions before the MLM head, so only T₄ is scored. The Hugging Face implementation, like the code in Section 8, passes all 8 rows through the head and ignores the unmasked rows in the loss (Figure 26). The loss is the same either way, because the head works on each row independently. 2. Word Embeddings This section answers three questions about word embeddings: what, how, and why. First, what are word embeddings? In simple terms, word embeddings are numerical representations of words or tokens in the form of vectors. Next, how are sentences converted into word embeddings? Take the example from the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) section. The sentence “BERT Stands for Bidirectional [MASK] Representation from Transformer” is broken down into tokens. Tokens are the smallest units of data, and can be words, special characters, or subwords. Figure 5: The WordPiece tokens and ids of the MLM sentence (top) and the 8-token running example used in this article (bottom). Figure 5 shows what the real WordPiece tokenizer does with that sentence. Common words like “stands” and “representation” are one token each, while “bidirectional” splits into four subword pieces and “transformer” into two, with ## marking a piece that continues a word. [CLS] and [SEP] are added at the start and the end, which gives 14 tokens. Every token has an id, its row number in the vocabulary, and [MASK] is id 103. To keep the figures readable, the rest of this article keeps one token per word, the 8 tokens in the lower panel. The shapes work the same way for 8 rows or 14. After that, these token ids are converted into vectors. An id is an index into the vocabulary, which is simply the collection of unique tokens, and it can be written as a one-hot vector : a vector of 30,522 values, all zero except a single 1 at the token’s index. Multiplying that one-hot vector by the embedding matrix gives the token’s vector, a 768-dimensional representation of the word or token. Equation 2: Word embedding lookup. Note: The numbers you see in the figures are coordinate indices or example values, for illustration. Figure 6: Word embeddings as a one-hot product and as a row lookup. Numbers are coordinate indices. In the upper half of Figure 6, the one-hot row for [MASK] has its 1 in column 103. E_word is the word-embedding matrix, 30,522 rows of 768, one row per vocabulary entry. Multiplying the one-hot row by E_word adds up every row of E_word weighted by 0, except row 103, which is weighted by 1. So the product is row 103, the [MASK] embedding x_4. This is why frameworks do not perform this multiplication explicitly: a one-hot product is a table lookup, and nn.Embedding does the lookup directly. The lower half does the same for all eight tokens at once. The 8 ids select 8 rows, and stacking them gives X_word, one row per token. In this example there are 8 tokens (in real-world scenarios, the number of tokens for this sentence differs, as Figure 5 showed), so the input embedding shape is (8, 768), where 768 is the dimension of the BERT Base model. Finally, why do we need word embeddings? Models (computers) cannot understand words. They only understand numbers. Therefore, words need to be converted into embeddings, which represent them in a multi-dimensional space. As humans, we can easily understand the meaning of words and the relationships between them. For example, we know that “happy” and “joy” have similar meanings. Models understand these relationships through vectors. In the multi-dimensional space, words with similar meanings are located close together, while words with unrelated meanings are far apart from each other. “Close” usually means pointing in a similar direction, and the standard way to measure it is the cosine similarity : Equation 3: Cosine similarity. Figure 7: Embeddings in two dimensions, with the cosine similarity of two pairs. Illustration. Figure 7 shows the idea in two dimensions. Words about technology sit together in the upper left, living things in the upper right, and short function words near the middle. “happy” and “joy” point almost the same way, a cosine of 0.99, while “happy” and “machine” point in nearly opposite directions, −0.89. The real space has 768 dimensions, but the measure is the same sum over coordinates. How do similar embeddings end up near each other in the multi-dimensional space? The answer is by training the model. Initially, the embeddings are randomly initialized. As the model trains, the loss pulls the vectors of tokens that are used in similar contexts toward similar positions, and tokens that are similar in meaning start to cluster together in the multi-dimensional space. The following code defines the word embedding layer in PyTorch: an nn.Embedding table with one 768-dimensional vector for each of the 30,522 WordPiece token ids. import torch import torch.nn as nn class TokenEmbedding(nn.Embedding): """E_word: one learned 768-vector per WordPiece id.""" def __init__(self, vocab_size=30522, embed_size=768): super().__init__(vocab_size, embed_size, padding_idx=0) # [PAD] has id 0 # vocab_size is 30,522 for bert-base-uncased and embed_size is 768, so # nn.Embedding creates a (30522, 768) table: 23.44 million learned numbers. 3. Position Embeddings Position embeddings give the model information about the position of each token in the sequence. Without them, the model would not be able to understand the position of a token in the sequence. Attention compares every token with every other token, and nothing in that comparison depends on order, so the same word in different positions would be treated the same. For example, in “BERT is a great model” and “Is BERT a great model?”, the word “BERT” appears in different positions, but without position embeddings the model would fail to recognize the difference. In BERT, position embeddings are created the same way as word embeddings, as a learned table, rather than with the sinusoidal function from the “Attention Is All You Need” paper. BERT has 512 position embeddings, which means only 512 tokens get their positional information. This is one of the reasons BERT cannot take long inputs directly, and why long documents have to be split into chunks. This positional information is learnable : it gets updated during backpropagation, and BERT learns the 512 positions during training. These position embeddings are absolute : each one represents a token’s position counted from the start of the sequence. Equation 4: Position embeddings. Figure 8: Learned position embeddings. An 8-token sequence reads the first 8 of 512 rows. On the left of Figure 8, E_pos is 512 rows of 768, one per position, and a sequence of 8 tokens takes the first 8 rows. That slice is P, one position vector per row of the input. The panel on the right is the example above. In "BERT is a great model", BERT sits at position 0 and its input is e_BERT + p_0. In "Is BERT a great model ?" it sits at position 1 and its input is e_BERT + p_1. The word vector is the same, but the position row is different, so the two inputs differ and the model can tell the sentences apart. The official BERT implementation is in TensorFlow. The following code shows the same logic in PyTorch: it creates the 512 × 768 position table, reads the rows for an 8-token sequence, and adds them to the word embeddings. # Official BERT code is TensorFlow; this is the same logic in PyTorch. See [3, 4]. seq_length = 8 # the running example max_position_embeddings = 512 embed_size = 768 # One learned row per position, created and trained for the maximum length (512) full_position_embeddings = nn.Embedding(max_position_embeddings, embed_size) # A sequence of 8 tokens reads only rows 0 ... 7 position_ids = torch.arange(seq_length, dtype=torch.long) # [0, 1, ..., 7] position_embeddings = full_position_embeddings(position_ids) # (8, 768) # Added point-wise to the word embeddings word_embeddings = TokenEmbedding()(torch.randint(1000, 30522, (seq_length,))) # (8, 768) input_embeddings = word_embeddings + position_embeddings # (8, 768) 4. Input Embeddings The word embeddings are added (point-wise addition) to the position embeddings. The segment embeddings are added as well (segment 0 for every token in a single sentence), and the sum is normalized with LayerNorm before it reaches the first encoder layer. These input embeddings carry both the word and its position in the sequence. Equation 5: Input embeddings. Figure 9: Input embeddings: word, position and segment embeddings added, then LayerNorm. In Figure 9, the three cards are all 8 × 768, so they add cell by cell. The highlighted cell is row 4, coordinate 0: the first number of the [MASK] word embedding, plus the first number of position 4, plus the first number of segment 0. Since every token here is in segment 0, S is the same row repeated 8 times. LayerNorm then rescales each row on its own (Section 6 shows how), and dropout is applied during training. The result X is the 8 × 768 input to the first encoder layer. The following code combines the word, position, and segment embeddings, then applies LayerNorm and dropout. When no segment ids are given, every token is assigned segment 0, as in our single-sentence example. class BertEmbeddings(nn.Module): """X = LayerNorm(E_word[t] + E_pos[0:n] + E_seg[s]), then dropout.""" def __init__(self, vocab_size=30522, d_model=768, max_len=512, n_segments=2, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() self.word = TokenEmbedding(vocab_size, d_model) self.position = nn.Embedding(max_len, d_model) self.segment = nn.Embedding(n_segments, d_model) self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model, eps=1e-12) self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) def forward(self, input_ids, segment_ids=None): # input_ids: (B, n) n = input_ids.size(1) pos_ids = torch.arange(n, device=input_ids.device) # 0 ... n-1 if segment_ids is None: # one sentence: segment 0 segment_ids = torch.zeros_like(input_ids) x = self.word(input_ids) + self.position(pos_ids) + self.segment(segment_ids) return self.dropout(self.norm(x)) # (B, n, 768) 5. Self Attention With the input embeddings in place, the next component is the self-attention mechanism . To fully understand multi-head attention, we first need to understand self-attention clearly. Self-attention has three key components: the Query , the Key , and the Value . All three are computed from the same input: the input embeddings in the first layer, or the output of the previous encoder layer after that. That shared source is what “self” means. In the full model, each of them comes from its own learned projection, which is the subject of Section 6. To see the mechanism on its own first, this section takes those projections to be the identity, so Q = K = V = X, each 8 × 768. What is self-attention? In simple terms, self-attention is a method where the input sequence is compared against itself to determine the importance of other words or tokens with respect to the current word. This allows the model to capture dependencies and relationships between words within the sequence, regardless of their positions. As a result, the model can understand the semantic and syntactic relationships between words in the input sequence. Equation 6: Scaled dot-product attention. Source: Attention Is All You Need. Equation 6 gives the mathematical form of self-attention. The Query matrix is multiplied by the transposed Key matrix, and the result is divided by the square root of the key dimension d_k (√768 in this section). Next, a softmax function is applied to each row of the resulting matrix. Finally, the output is multiplied by the Value matrix, which gives the self-attention output. Figure 10: One self-attention layer, single head, with Q = K = V = X. Figure 10 is Equation 6 in blocks. X is copied into Q, K and V. Q and K meet in the score block, which compares every pair of tokens and returns S, 8 × 8. The softmax turns each row of S into weights A that add up to 1, and A multiplies V to give Z, the same 8 × 768 shape as X. The dashed identity boxes are where Section 6 places its weight matrices. Equation 7: Attention scores. Figure 11: Self-attention part 1, the scores QKᵀ / √768. Numbers are coordinate indices. As shown in Figure 11, the Query and the transposed Key matrices are multiplied and divided by √768 = 27.71. The resulting matrix is 8 × 8 and holds the attention logits of each token with every other token in the sequence. The highlighted row 4 of Q is the [MASK] token's query, and the highlighted column 3 of Kᵀ is the key of "Bidirectional". Their dot product, 768 multiplications added up, is the single score S₄,₃. Every other cell of S is the same calculation with a different row and column. Without the division, dot products of 768-dimensional vectors become large, and the softmax would push almost all of the weight onto one token and pass back very small gradients. Equation 8: Row-wise softmax. Figure 12: Self-attention part 2, the row-wise softmax. Example values. The resulting matrix is then fed into a softmax function, which outputs a set of probabilities, the attention scores . These attention scores show how much each token depends on the other tokens in the sequence, through semantic and syntactic relationships. In other words, they show how important each token is to every other token in the sequence. Figure 12 uses example values. Because Q = K in this section, S is symmetric, and the diagonal is the largest entry in every row, since a vector is most similar to itself. This is one more reason the real model gives queries and keys their own projections. After the softmax, the [MASK] row puts 0.409 on itself, 0.193 on "Bidirectional", 0.166 on "Representation", and the remaining 0.232 on the other five tokens. Every row adds up to 1.000, as the column on the right shows. Equation 9: Self-attention output. Figure 13: Self-attention part 3, the output Z = AV. Then the attention matrix (8, 8) is multiplied by the Value matrix (8, 768), which gives the attention output (8, 768). In this output, each token’s row now holds information from the other tokens. As Figure 13 writes out for row 4, the [MASK] token's new vector z_4 is a weighted sum of all eight value rows, with the weights from Figure 12. Most of it comes from its own row and its two neighbors, "Bidirectional" and "Representation", which is the context it needs to predict the missing word. This combined information then moves on through the rest of the layer. The following code implements Equation 6. The optional mask is a padding mask, not a causal mask, so every token can still attend to every other token in the sequence. import math import torch.nn.functional as F class Attention(nn.Module): """softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V (Equation 6).""" def forward(self, query, key, value, mask=None, dropout=None): scores = torch.matmul(query, key.transpose(-2, -1)) \ / math.sqrt(query.size(-1)) # S, (..., n, n) if mask is not None: # padding mask, never causal scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9) p_attn = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) # A, every row sums to 1 if dropout is not None: p_attn = dropout(p_attn) return torch.matmul(p_attn, value), p_attn # Z = A V, and A 6. Multi-Head Attention Self-attention captures the relationships between words. Then why do we need multi-head attention ? Self-attention captures the relationships between words from one perspective (it may capture the order of the sequence, grammatical structure, context, or dependencies between words). Multi-head attention captures the relationships between words from several perspectives at once, with the help of learned weights (parameters). Self-attention above works at the model dimension, while multi-head attention works at each head’s dimension. Equation 10: Multi-head attention. Source: Attention Is All You Need paper. The Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V) all come from the same input, the input embeddings or the output of the previous encoder layer. BERT Base’s model dimension is 768, and the multi-head attention layer has 12 heads. To calculate the dimension of each head, we divide 768 by 12, which gives 64. For each of these 12 heads, we need three components: the query, key, and value matrices. This means there are 12 separate attention mechanisms in the multi-head attention layer, and each one captures a different perspective of the input sequence. These query, key, and value matrices are created with weight matrices. As shown in Equation 10 and illustrated in Figures 14 and 15, to create the query matrices, we multiply the input by 12 query weight matrices, each of size (768, 64). In practice this is organized a little differently, as explained in the code section. This gives 12 query matrices, one for each head, each of size (8, 64). Here, 64 is the dimension of the head, and 8 is the number of tokens in our example. The same process is repeated to create the key and value matrices for all heads. Each of these weight matrices is a linear layer. Equation 11: The linear layer as computed by torch.nn.Linear. Figure 14: A linear layer as matrices, nn.Linear(768, 3072). Important note to understand the linear layer: PyTorch stores the weight matrix as (current layer’s number of neurons, previous layer’s or input layer’s number of neurons), that is, output size × input size. We initialize the layer with the input size and the output size, nn.Linear(input vector size, output vector size). For example, the FFN of BERT Base has 768 input units and 3072 neurons in its hidden layer, so nn.Linear(768, 3072) holds a weight matrix W of size (3072, 768). The input vectors are multiplied by this matrix, transposed, which gives new vectors, and then the bias vector is added. This is a linear transformation of vectors: they move from one dimension (768) to another (3072), or to the same dimension. Equation 11 is the linear layer operation in PyTorch. As emphasized in my previous articles, when it comes to linear layers or neural networks, it is essential to think in terms of matrices and vectors rather than neurons. In Figure 14, the input row x (768 numbers) is multiplied by Wᵀ, 768 rows of 3072. Column 2 of Wᵀ, which is row 2 of the stored W, dotted with x, plus the bias b_2, gives the output coordinate y_2, and each of the 3072 outputs is one such dot product. When x has 8 rows instead of one, the same bias row is added to every row of the result, which is called broadcasting . Equation 12: Per-head projections in BERT Base. Figure 15: Query, key and value projections for each head. The top of Figure 15 is head 1’s query with all its indices. X is 8 × 768, W₁^Q is 768 × 64, and Q₁ is 8 × 64: each token keeps its row, but the row is now 64 numbers. The bottom half shows all 36 projections at once, 12 heads for each of query, key and value, with every weight 768 × 64 = 49,152 numbers and every output 8 × 64. Figure 16: Multi-head notation: 12 heads, each with its own Q, K and V of 8 × 64 Figure 16 lays out the result per head. Each head holds its own Q_h, K_h and V_h, all 8 × 64. Every head sees all 8 tokens but only its own 64 coordinates, and 12 × 64 = 768 brings the heads back to the model dimension. Within each head, the same self-attention operation from Section 5 takes place, using that head’s query, key, and value matrices. Taking the first head as an example, the Q₁ matrix (8, 64) is multiplied by the transposed K₁ matrix (64, 8), resulting in an 8 × 8 matrix. Next, this matrix is divided by the square root of the key’s dimension, which is 8 (since the key’s dimension is 64). The softmax is applied to each row, and the result is multiplied by the value matrix V₁, producing the attention output for head 1, with a size of (8, 64). Equation 13: Attention inside one head. Figure 17: Attention inside each head. The attention maps are example patterns. This same operation is repeated for all 12 heads, generating 12 attention head outputs, each of size (8, 64). Figure 17 shows why several heads help, with example attention maps. One head may learn to look one token back, another one token ahead, and another lets the [MASK] row gather from "Bidirectional", "Representation" and "Transformer" on both sides. Each head can learn its own pattern because each has its own weights, and studies of trained BERT models have found heads that specialize in this way. Figure 18: Concatenating the 12 heads, then the output projection W^O. Finally, the outputs from all the heads are concatenated, resulting in a single output of size (8, 768). In Figure 18, head 1 fills columns 0–63, head 2 columns 64–127, and head 12 columns 704–767. The concatenated output is linearly projected with a weight matrix W^O of size (768, 768), giving the multi-head attention layer output of size (8, 768). Concatenation only places the heads side by side. W^O is the step that mixes them, so every coordinate of the output can draw on every head. The PyTorch implementation follows the same mathematics, with one difference in how the weights are organized, shown in Figure 19. Figure 19: How the code computes all 12 heads with one projection and a reshape. Instead of 12 separate 768 × 64 matrices, the code keeps one 768 × 768 matrix per role, with the 12 head matrices side by side. One product X W^Q gives an 8 × 768 Q whose columns 0–63 are exactly Q₁, columns 64–127 are Q₂, and so on. .view(B, n, 12, 64) splits each token's 768 numbers into 12 groups of 64, and .transpose(1, 2) moves the head axis in front of the tokens, giving one 8 × 64 matrix per head. Both ways give the same queries and the same number of parameters, but the fused version is one large matrix product instead of twelve small ones. The following code snippet will give you a better understanding of how MHA works in practice. class MultiHeadedAttention(nn.Module): def __init__(self, h=12, d_model=768, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() assert d_model % h == 0 # 768 / 12 = 64, so the heads tile d_model exactly self.d_k = d_model // h # head dimension, 64 self.h = h # number of heads, 12 # W^Q, W^K, W^V: each one nn.Linear(768, 768) = 12 heads of (768, 64) side by side self.linear_layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(d_model, d_model) for _ in range(3)]) self.output_linear = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model) # W^O, (768, 768) self.attention = Attention() self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout) def forward(self, query, key, value, mask=None): # each (B, n, 768), all X in BERT batch_size = query.size(0) # B, the batch size """ The theory (Figure 15) uses 12 separate (768, 64) weight matrices per role. In practice one nn.Linear(768, 768) holds all 12 side by side (Figure 19). One matrix product gives (B, n, 768), .view splits the 768 columns into 12 heads of 64, and .transpose moves the head axis in front of the tokens. Same outputs and the same parameter count, in one matrix product. """ # 1) project, then split: (B, n, 768) -> (B, n, 12, 64) -> (B, 12, n, 64) query, key, value = [l(x).view(batch_size, -1, self.h, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2) for l, x in zip(self.linear_layers, (query, key, value))] # 2) attention in all 12 heads at once: (B, 12, n, 64) x, attn = self.attention(query, key, value, mask=mask, dropout=self.dropout) # 3) concat: (B, 12, n, 64) -> (B, n, 12, 64) -> (B, n, 768) x = x.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(batch_size, -1, self.h * self.d_k) return self.output_linear(x) # W^O, (B, n, 768) One more step comes before the feed-forward network: the Add & Norm block that follows attention in Figure 3. Equation 14: Add & Norm, and LayerNorm. Figure 20: Add & Norm after multi-head attention, with LayerNorm on one row. The attention output is added to the layer’s own input, which is the residual connection , and the sum is normalized. LayerNorm works on each token’s row by itself, as Figure 20 shows for row 4. It computes the mean μ₄ and the variance σ₄² of the row’s 768 numbers, subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, and then scales and shifts the result with γ and β, two learned 768-vectors shared by every token. BERT applies the normalization after the addition (post-norm), the arrangement used in the original Transformer. The same block follows the feed-forward network. 7. Feed Forward Network In its simplest form, a feed-forward network is a type of neural network that consists of three layers: an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer. The number of input units in the input layer and the number of neurons in the output layer equal the model’s dimension (768). In the case of BERT, the hidden layer is four times (3072) the model’s dimension. The FFN (Feed Forward Network) has a different role from attention. The attention mechanism gathers information from across the sequence. The attention layer captures the semantic and syntactic relationships between words and builds a contextual understanding of the sequence. The Feed Forward Network then processes that gathered information for each token on its own. It holds most of the model’s parameters, more than half of BERT Base (Figure 27), and it learns the patterns of the language humans use to communicate. By learning them, the model can predict the tokens. Equation 15: The feed-forward network of BERT Base. Figure 21: The feed-forward network of BERT Base drawn as neurons. The output from the multi-head attention layer, after Add & Norm, has a size of (8, 768) and is fed into the input layer of the Feed-Forward Network (FFN). Think of the input layer as a bridge that simply passes on the information without performing any operation. Figure 21 shows the network as neurons, for one token. Each of the 3072 hidden units is connected to all 768 inputs, which is a 3072 × 768 weight matrix, and each of the 768 outputs is connected to all 3072 hidden units, a 768 × 3072 matrix. That is 2.36 million parameters on each side. Figure 22: The feed-forward network on one token. Numbers are coordinate indices Figure 22 shows the same token as matrices. Row 2 of W₁ dotted with x, plus the bias, then passed through GELU, gives the hidden coordinate h₂, and all 3072 rows together give h. W₂ takes h back to a 768-vector y. The hidden layer is four times wider than the token, which gives the nonlinearity room to work. For the whole sequence, the input (8, 768) is multiplied by the transpose of the FFN hidden-layer weight matrix, which is stored with a size of (3072, 768), resulting in a matrix of size (8, 3072). Next, a bias vector (1, 3072) is added to each row of the resulting matrix, a process known as broadcasting. GELU applied to this matrix gives the hidden layer output. Figure 23: FFN hidden layer and output layer operations on the whole sequence. The output from the hidden layer (8, 3072) is then multiplied by the transpose of the FFN output-layer weight matrix, stored with a size of (768, 3072), resulting in a matrix of size (8, 768). Finally, an output-layer bias vector (1, 768) is added to each row, completing the FFN layer output. Both halves are shown in Figure 23. Every token passes through the same weights, independently of the others, which is why the “Attention Is All You Need” paper calls it position-wise. After Add & Norm, this output is passed on to the next encoder layer, or to the MLM head after the last layer. The bias vectors give every unit a learned offset, so a neuron can still be active when its weighted input adds up to zero. In BERT, the GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) activation function is used. GELU weights each input by the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is smaller than it, x·Φ(x), which makes it a smooth version of ReLU. It can be approximated with the tanh formula in Equation 16, or more simply as GELU ≈ x·sigmoid(1.702x). Equation 16: GELU and its two approximations. Figure 24: GELU, its tanh and sigmoid approximations, and ReLU. In Figure 24, GELU is almost the identity for large positive inputs and almost 0 for large negative inputs, like ReLU. In between, it bends smoothly and dips slightly below zero, to −0.170 at x = −0.75, so small negative inputs still pass a little signal and a gradient. The tanh form, which the original BERT code uses, stays within 0.0005 of the exact curve. The sigmoid form is simpler and stays within about 0.02. The following code implements the FFN and one encoder layer. With both halves in place, one encoder layer is attention and the FFN, each wrapped in Add & Norm, and BERT Base stacks 12 of them. class PositionwiseFeedForward(nn.Module): # d_model is the model dimension (768), d_ff the hidden size (3072) def __init__(self, d_model=768, d_ff=3072): super().__init__() self.w_1 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff) # W_1: weight (3072, 768), bias (3072) self.w_2 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model) # W_2: weight (768, 3072), bias (768) self.activation = nn.GELU() # x * Phi(x), Equation 16 def forward(self, x): # (B, n, 768) return self.w_2(self.activation(self.w_1(x))) # (B, n, 3072) -> (B, n, 768) class EncoderLayer(nn.Module): """Post-norm, as in BERT: X' = LN(X + MHA(X)), X'' = LN(X' + FFN(X')).""" def __init__(self, d_model=768, h=12, d_ff=3072, dropout=0.1): super().__init__() self.attention = MultiHeadedAttention(h, d_model, dropout) self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model, eps=1e-12) self.ffn = PositionwiseFeedForward(d_model, d_ff) self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model, eps=1e-12) self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) def forward(self, x, mask=None): # (B, n, 768) x = self.norm1(x + self.dropout(self.attention(x, x, x, mask))) # Add & Norm 1 return self.norm2(x + self.dropout(self.ffn(x))) # Add & Norm 2 8. Linear Layer and Softmax in MLM After all the encoder layers (12), the final matrix (8, 768) is fed into the MLM head to predict the exact token for the Masked Language Model (MLM) task. The head has two parts: a transform, which is a 768 × 768 dense layer with GELU and LayerNorm, and then the output linear layer, whose weight is the word-embedding matrix itself, transposed. Equation 17: The MLM head. Figure 25: The output layer of the MLM head, tied to the word embeddings. Figure 25 shows the output layer as neurons. Each of the 30,522 outputs is connected to all 768 inputs, so its weight matrix is 768 × 30,522, the same size as the word-embedding table. BERT does not learn a second table. It reuses E_word ( weight tying ) and adds only a bias of 30,522 numbers, so the vector that represents a word at the input is also the one its output score is measured against. Figure 26: The MLM head, from the last hidden state to the predicted token and the loss. Example probabilities In Figure 26, the (8, 768) matrix is first transformed, row by row, into H̃. H̃ is then multiplied by E_wordᵀ (768, 30,522), and the bias is added. This results in a new matrix with a size of (8, 30,522), where 30,522 is the total number of tokens in the vocabulary. This resulting matrix is called the logits matrix. All 8 rows pass through the head here, as in the Hugging Face implementation, and only row 4 is used in the loss. Next, the softmax function is applied to the logits matrix, which assigns a probability to every vocabulary token, row by row. The index with the highest probability score is selected as the output token. When the masked token’s vector (in this case, the 5th token, index 4) passes through the head, it produces a logit vector of size (1, 30,522). This vector is then fed into the softmax function, which generates probability scores across all 30,522 possible tokens. In our example, the correct output is the token “Encoder”, so the probability in its column should be high for the model to output “Encoder”: 0.62 in the example values of Figure 26. This means the model is confident that the correct output is “Encoder”. (In the real vocabulary, “encoder” is three WordPiece tokens, en, ##code and ##r, and each of those masked positions would get its own row and its own prediction.) The loss is computed on the same row. The target is a one-hot row, all zeros except a one at the target index. Cross-entropy against it picks out the log-probability of the correct token, as Equation 18 shows. It is computed only at the masked positions, here row 4, and its gradient is what trains every weight in the model for the task. Equation 18: Prediction and cross-entropy loss at the masked position. The following code implements the MLM head. The output layer’s weight is assigned the word-embedding table, so the input embeddings and the output layer share the same (30522, 768) parameters. class MaskedLanguageModel(nn.Module): # hidden --> model dimension (768), vocab_size --> 30522 def __init__(self, word_embeddings, hidden=768): super().__init__() self.transform = nn.Linear(hidden, hidden) # W_t, (768, 768) self.activation = nn.GELU() self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden, eps=1e-12) vocab_size = word_embeddings.num_embeddings self.decoder = nn.Linear(hidden, vocab_size, bias=False) self.decoder.weight = word_embeddings.weight # tied: the same (30522, 768) table self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(vocab_size)) # the only new output parameters self.softmax = nn.LogSoftmax(dim=-1) def forward(self, x): # (B, n, 768) x = self.norm(self.activation(self.transform(x))) return self.softmax(self.decoder(x) + self.bias) # log-probs, (B, n, 30522) The last block puts every piece from this article together and runs the eight-token example. With the weights of Hugging Face’s BertForMaskedLM copied in, its log-probabilities agree to within 3 × 10⁻⁶, and the parameter counts are identical. class BERT(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size=30522, d_model=768, n_layers=12, h=12, d_ff=3072): super().__init__() self.embeddings = BertEmbeddings(vocab_size, d_model) self.layers = nn.ModuleList([EncoderLayer(d_model, h, d_ff) for _ in range(n_layers)]) self.mlm = MaskedLanguageModel(self.embeddings.word, d_model) def forward(self, input_ids, mask=None): x = self.embeddings(input_ids) # (B, n, 768) for layer in self.layers: x = layer(x, mask) # (B, n, 768), 12 times return self.mlm(x) # (B, n, 30522) model = BERT().eval() ids = torch.randint(1000, 30522, (1, 8)) # any 8 token ids ids[0, 4] = 103 # [MASK] at position 4, as in the figures log_p = model(ids) print(log_p.shape) # torch.Size([1, 8, 30522]) print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())) # 109514298 Figure 27: Where BERT Base’s 109.48 million parameters live. Figure 27 counts the parameters by component. The 12 feed-forward networks hold just over half of BERT Base, the 12 attention layers about a quarter, and the word-embedding table a fifth. Positions, segments, and all the LayerNorms together come to under half a percent. Important note: The weight matrices, bias vectors, LayerNorm parameters, position embeddings, and word embeddings are all learnable. They get updated during the backpropagation process while the model is being trained. Conclusion Some topics were not covered in this article, such as segment embeddings, the next-sentence prediction task, and fine-tuning BERT for specific tasks. However, it covers the most essential topics for a solid understanding of the BERT architecture: word and position embeddings, the masked language model task, self-attention and multi-head attention, the feed-forward network, and the linear and softmax layers of the MLM head. By understanding the architecture, you can modify the loss function and the BERT architecture to suit your specific use case, and tailor BERT to your needs. BERT: In-Depth Exploration of Architecture, Workflow, Code, and Mathematical FoundationsEmbeddings, Masked Language Model Tasks, Attention Mechanisms, and Feed-Forward Networks Explained Through Equations, Matrix Transformations, and Code

BERT was introduced in 2018, and it has been a topic of interest for many, with lots of articles and YouTube videos explaining it. This article explains BERT through its architecture, workflow, code, and mathematical foundations, and follows one example sentence through every matrix transformation, from the word embeddings to the softmax output. Whether you are looking to deepen your existing knowledge of BERT or are just starting your career in AI, this article aims to give you a complete understanding of it.

Linkedin: jaiganesan-n 🌏❤️

Before going into how BERT works, we need to understand the difference between BERT and today’s LLMs, because both use the Transformer architecture.

An LLM is a probabilistic, auto-regressive model. Auto-regressive means the LLM is trained to predict the next token (the next-token prediction task) from the current context. It gets this property from a causal mask in the attention layer, which lets each token attend only to the tokens before it (left context), never to the tokens after it. That is what allows the model to predict the next token from the current and previous tokens.

BERT does not use a causal mask, so each token attends to the other tokens in both directions (left and right context). The objective of BERT is also different. It was designed and trained on two tasks, the Masked Language Model (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). After pre-training, BERT can be fine-tuned for tasks such as classification and question answering.

Figure 1: The causal mask of a decoder (left) and BERT’s bidirectional attention (right) on the running example.

Figure 1 places the difference on one grid. Each row is the token doing the looking, and each column is the token being looked at. On the left, the decoder sets every score above the diagonal to −∞ before the softmax, so the [MASK] row can see only the five tokens up to itself. On the right, BERT keeps all 64 cells, and the [MASK] row reads "Bidirectional" before it and "Representation from Transformer" after it. This second pattern is the reason BERT is good at filling in a blank.

Two BERT architectures were released in 2018, BERT Base and BERT Large. A Transformer with this bidirectional attention is usually called an Encoder model. A Transformer with the causal mask applied (left context only) is usually called a Decoder model, the family today’s LLMs belong to. Both BERT models use the WordPiece tokenizer, which has a vocabulary of 30,522 tokens for the uncased models.

  • BERT Base: 12 encoder layers, 12 attention heads, a feed-forward hidden size of 3072, and about 110M parameters in total. The embedding size is 768.
  • BERT Large: 24 encoder layers, 16 attention heads, a feed-forward hidden size of 4096, and about 340M parameters in total. The embedding size is 1024.
Figure 2: BERT Base and BERT Large. Parameter counts from the Hugging Face BertModel at each configuration.

Figure 2 lines the two up. The head dimension is 64 in both, because 768 / 12 and 1024 / 16 are both 64, and the feed-forward hidden size is four times the model dimension in both. The paper’s 110M and 340M are rounded values. Counting the actual weights gives 109.48M and 335.14M.

In this article, we explore BERT based on the BERT Base architecture and its properties.

A note on the figures: Each figure shows a transformation: the tensors going in, the operation, and the tensor coming out, labeled with the symbols the equations use and with the equation the figure draws set above it. To keep the shapes concrete, every figure uses one running example: the MLM sentence from Section 1, cut into 8 tokens, one per word. The sizes are those of BERT Base: model dimension d = 768, 12 heads of d_k = 64, feed-forward hidden size d_ff = 3072, a vocabulary of 30,522, and 512 positions. A sequence is a matrix with one row per token, so the input to every encoder layer is 8 × 768. The numbers inside the vectors and along the edges of the matrices are coordinate indices, 0 up to 767, so you can follow one coordinate through a product. The exceptions are the attention scores, the softmax weights, and the predicted probabilities, where the values are the point. Those are example values, and each figure says so. Weight matrices are pink, inputs blue, hidden activations peach, outputs green, and the row or column being followed is yellow.
Figure 3: BERT Base end to end, with the shape on every arrow. Running example: 8 tokens, d = 768.

Figure 3 shows the BERT Base architecture end to end, from word embeddings to the linear and softmax layers. Eight token ids are looked up in the word-embedding table, added to the position embeddings and the segment embeddings (segment 0 for every token in a single sentence), and normalized. The resulting 8 × 768 matrix passes through 12 identical encoder layers. Each layer is multi-head attention and a feed-forward network, and each of the two is followed by Add & Norm. The MLM head at the end turns every 768-vector back into a score for each of the 30,522 vocabulary entries. Every arrow between the encoder layers carries the same 8 × 768 shape. Only the embeddings at the start and the MLM head at the end change it.

BERT was specifically designed for the Masked Language Model (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) tasks. Here, we focus only on the MLM task to understand the BERT Base architecture.

Note: This article does not go into segment embeddings from an architectural or theoretical perspective, because it explores BERT through the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) task, which can be explained on a single sentence. Segment embeddings mark which sentence of a pair a token belongs to, which is what the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task needs. BERT still adds them for a single sentence. Every token is then in segment 0, so the segment embedding is the same row for every token. Figure 3, Figure 9, Equation 5, and the code in Section 4 include it to keep the shapes accurate.
1. Masked Language Model (MLM)

The Masked Language Model task is a Cloze task: we train the model to fill in the blanks in a sentence. To illustrate this, take a simple example, the sentence “BERT Stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformer”.

In this sentence, we remove the word “Encoder” and replace it with a special [MASK] token that marks the blank. The resulting sentence is "BERT Stands for Bidirectional [MASK] Representation from Transformer". We give this sentence to BERT and train the model to predict the token "Encoder". By understanding the rest of the input, the model predicts the missing token.

In pre-training, BERT picks 15% of the token positions at random. Of those, 80% are replaced with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and 10% are left unchanged, so the model cannot learn to pay attention only when it sees [MASK]. Our example masks one token.

Figure 4: The masked language model task on one sentence. Only the masked position enters the loss. The probabilities are example values.

In Figure 4, the eight input tokens enter at the bottom, with [MASK] at position 4. The encoder returns one 768-vector per position, T₀ to T₇, and every one of them has seen the whole sentence.
