2. Word Embeddings

This section answers three questions about word embeddings: what, how, and why. First, what are word embeddings? In simple terms, word embeddings are numerical representations of words or tokens in the form of vectors.

Next, how are sentences converted into word embeddings? Take the example from the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) section. The sentence “BERT Stands for Bidirectional [MASK] Representation from Transformer” is broken down into tokens. Tokens are the smallest units of data, and can be words, special characters, or subwords.

Figure 5: The WordPiece tokens and ids of the MLM sentence (top) and the 8-token running example used in this article (bottom).

Figure 5 shows what the real WordPiece tokenizer does with that sentence. Common words like “stands” and “representation” are one token each, while “bidirectional” splits into four subword pieces and “transformer” into two, with ## marking a piece that continues a word. [CLS] and [SEP] are added at the start and the end, which gives 14 tokens. Every token has an id, its row number in the vocabulary, and [MASK] is id 103. To keep the figures readable, the rest of this article keeps one token per word, the 8 tokens in the lower panel. The shapes work the same way for 8 rows or 14.

After that, these token ids are converted into vectors. An id is an index into the vocabulary, which is simply the collection of unique tokens, and it can be written as a one-hot vector: a vector of 30,522 values, all zero except a single 1 at the token’s index. Multiplying that one-hot vector by the embedding matrix gives the token’s vector, a 768-dimensional representation of the word or token.

Equation 2: Word embedding lookup.
Note: The numbers you see in the figures are coordinate indices or example values, for illustration.
Figure 6: Word embeddings as a one-hot product and as a row lookup. Numbers are coordinate indices.

In the upper half of Figure 6, the one-hot row for [MASK] has its 1 in column 103. E_word is the word-embedding matrix, 30,522 rows of 768, one row per vocabulary entry. Multiplying the one-hot row by E_word adds up every row of E_word weighted by 0, except row 103, which is weighted by 1. So the product is row 103, the [MASK] embedding x_4. This is why frameworks do not perform this multiplication explicitly: a one-hot product is a table lookup, and nn.Embedding does the lookup directly.

The lower half does the same for all eight tokens at once. The 8 ids select 8 rows, and stacking them gives X_word, one row per token. In this example there are 8 tokens (in real-world scenarios, the number of tokens for this sentence differs, as Figure 5 showed), so the input embedding shape is (8, 768), where 768 is the dimension of the BERT Base model.

Finally, why do we need word embeddings? Models (computers) cannot understand words. They only understand numbers. Therefore, words need to be converted into embeddings, which represent them in a multi-dimensional space.

As humans, we can easily understand the meaning of words and the relationships between them. For example, we know that “happy” and “joy” have similar meanings. Models understand these relationships through vectors. In the multi-dimensional space, words with similar meanings are located close together, while words with unrelated meanings are far apart from each other. “Close” usually means pointing in a similar direction, and the standard way to measure it is the cosine similarity:

Equation 3: Cosine similarity.Figure 7: Embeddings in two dimensions, with the cosine similarity of two pairs. Illustration.

Figure 7 shows the idea in two dimensions. Words about technology sit together in the upper left, living things in the upper right, and short function words near the middle. “happy” and “joy” point almost the same way, a cosine of 0.99, while “happy” and “machine” point in nearly opposite directions, −0.89. The real space has 768 dimensions, but the measure is the same sum over coordinates.

How do similar embeddings end up near each other in the multi-dimensional space? The answer is by training the model. Initially, the embeddings are randomly initialized. As the model trains, the loss pulls the vectors of tokens that are used in similar contexts toward similar positions, and tokens that are similar in meaning start to cluster together in the multi-dimensional space.

The following code defines the word embedding layer in PyTorch: an nn.Embedding table with one 768-dimensional vector for each of the 30,522 WordPiece token ids.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class TokenEmbedding(nn.Embedding):
    """E_word: one learned 768-vector per WordPiece id."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=30522, embed_size=768):
        super().__init__(vocab_size, embed_size, padding_idx=0)   # [PAD] has id 0
# vocab_size is 30,522 for bert-base-uncased and embed_size is 768, so
# nn.Embedding creates a (30522, 768) table: 23.44 million learned numbers.
3. Position Embeddings

Position embeddings give the model information about the position of each token in the sequence. Without them, the model would not be able to understand the position of a token in the sequence. Attention compares every token with every other token, and nothing in that comparison depends on order, so the same word in different positions would be treated the same. For example, in “BERT is a great model” and “Is BERT a great model?”, the word “BERT” appears in different positions, but without position embeddings the model would fail to recognize the difference.

In BERT, position embeddings are created the same way as word embeddings, as a learned table, rather than with the sinusoidal function from the “Attention Is All You Need” paper. BERT has 512 position embeddings, which means only 512 tokens get their positional information. This is one of the reasons BERT cannot take long inputs directly, and why long documents have to be split into chunks. This positional information is learnable: it gets updated during backpropagation, and BERT learns the 512 positions during training. These position embeddings are absolute: each one represents a token’s position counted from the start of the sequence.

Equation 4: Position embeddings.Figure 8: Learned position embeddings. An 8-token sequence reads the first 8 of 512 rows.

On the left of Figure 8, E_pos is 512 rows of 768, one per position, and a sequence of 8 tokens takes the first 8 rows. That slice is P, one position vector per row of the input. The panel on the right is the example above. In "BERT is a great model", BERT sits at position 0 and its input is e_BERT + p_0. In "Is BERT a great model ?" it sits at position 1 and its input is e_BERT + p_1. The word vector is the same, but the position row is different, so the two inputs differ and the model can tell the sentences apart.

The official BERT implementation is in TensorFlow. The following code shows the same logic in PyTorch: it creates the 512 × 768 position table, reads the rows for an 8-token sequence, and adds them to the word embeddings.

# Official BERT code is TensorFlow; this is the same logic in PyTorch. See [3, 4].
seq_length = 8                     # the running example
max_position_embeddings = 512
embed_size = 768

# One learned row per position, created and trained for the maximum length (512)
full_position_embeddings = nn.Embedding(max_position_embeddings, embed_size)
# A sequence of 8 tokens reads only rows 0 ... 7
position_ids = torch.arange(seq_length, dtype=torch.long)        # [0, 1, ..., 7]
position_embeddings = full_position_embeddings(position_ids)      # (8, 768)
# Added point-wise to the word embeddings
word_embeddings = TokenEmbedding()(torch.randint(1000, 30522, (seq_length,)))   # (8, 768)
input_embeddings = word_embeddings + position_embeddings                          # (8, 768)
4. Input Embeddings

The word embeddings are added (point-wise addition) to the position embeddings. The segment embeddings are added as well (segment 0 for every token in a single sentence), and the sum is normalized with LayerNorm before it reaches the first encoder layer. These input embeddings carry both the word and its position in the sequence.

Equation 5: Input embeddings.Figure 9: Input embeddings: word, position and segment embeddings added, then LayerNorm.

In Figure 9, the three cards are all 8 × 768, so they add cell by cell. The highlighted cell is row 4, coordinate 0: the first number of the [MASK] word embedding, plus the first number of position 4, plus the first number of segment 0. Since every token here is in segment 0, S is the same row repeated 8 times. LayerNorm then rescales each row on its own (Section 6 shows how), and dropout is applied during training. The result X is the 8 × 768 input to the first encoder layer.

The following code combines the word, position, and segment embeddings, then applies LayerNorm and dropout. When no segment ids are given, every token is assigned segment 0, as in our single-sentence example.

class BertEmbeddings(nn.Module):
    """X = LayerNorm(E_word[t] + E_pos[0:n] + E_seg[s]), then dropout."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=30522, d_model=768, max_len=512, n_segments=2,
                 dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.word = TokenEmbedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position = nn.Embedding(max_len, d_model)
        self.segment = nn.Embedding(n_segments, d_model)
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model, eps=1e-12)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

def forward(self, input_ids, segment_ids=None):            # input_ids: (B, n)
        n = input_ids.size(1)
        pos_ids = torch.arange(n, device=input_ids.device)       # 0 ... n-1
        if segment_ids is None:                                  # one sentence: segment 0
            segment_ids = torch.zeros_like(input_ids)
        x = self.word(input_ids) + self.position(pos_ids) + self.segment(segment_ids)
        return self.dropout(self.norm(x))                        # (B, n, 768)
5. Self Attention

With the input embeddings in place, the next component is the self-attention mechanism. To fully understand multi-head attention, we first need to understand self-attention clearly.

Self-attention has three key components: the Query, the Key, and the Value. All three are computed from the same input: the input embeddings in the first layer, or the output of the previous encoder layer after that. That shared source is what “self” means. In the full model, each of them comes from its own learned projection, which is the subject of Section 6. To see the mechanism on its own first, this section takes those projections to be the identity, so Q = K = V = X, each 8 × 768.

What is self-attention?

In simple terms, self-attention is a method where the input sequence is compared against itself to determine the importance of other words or tokens with respect to the current word. This allows the model to capture dependencies and relationships between words within the sequence, regardless of their positions. As a result, the model can understand the semantic and syntactic relationships between words in the input sequence.

Equation 6: Scaled dot-product attention. Source: Attention Is All You Need.

Equation 6 gives the mathematical form of self-attention. The Query matrix is multiplied by the transposed Key matrix, and the result is divided by the square root of the key dimension d_k (√768 in this section). Next, a softmax function is applied to each row of the resulting matrix. Finally, the output is multiplied by the Value matrix, which gives the self-attention output.

Figure 10: One self-attention layer, single head, with Q = K = V = X.

Figure 10 is Equation 6 in blocks. X is copied into Q, K and V. Q and K meet in the score block, which compares every pair of tokens and returns S, 8 × 8. The softmax turns each row of S into weights A that add up to 1, and A multiplies V to give Z, the same 8 × 768 shape as X. The dashed identity boxes are where Section 6 places its weight matrices.

Equation 7: Attention scores.Figure 11: Self-attention part 1, the scores QKᵀ / √768. Numbers are coordinate indices.

As shown in Figure 11, the Query and the transposed Key matrices are multiplied and divided by √768 = 27.71. The resulting matrix is 8 × 8 and holds the attention logits of each token with every other token in the sequence. The highlighted row 4 of Q is the [MASK] token's query, and the highlighted column 3 of Kᵀ is the key of "Bidirectional". Their dot product, 768 multiplications added up, is the single score S₄,₃. Every other cell of S is the same calculation with a different row and column. Without the division, dot products of 768-dimensional vectors become large, and the softmax would push almost all of the weight onto one token and pass back very small gradients.

Equation 8: Row-wise softmax.Figure 12: Self-attention part 2, the row-wise softmax. Example values.

The resulting matrix is then fed into a softmax function, which outputs a set of probabilities, the attention scores. These attention scores show how much each token depends on the other tokens in the sequence, through semantic and syntactic relationships. In other words, they show how important each token is to every other token in the sequence.

Figure 12 uses example values. Because Q = K in this section, S is symmetric, and the diagonal is the largest entry in every row, since a vector is most similar to itself. This is one more reason the real model gives queries and keys their own projections. After the softmax, the [MASK] row puts 0.409 on itself, 0.193 on "Bidirectional", 0.166 on "Representation", and the remaining 0.232 on the other five tokens. Every row adds up to 1.000, as the column on the right shows.

Equation 9: Self-attention output.Figure 13: Self-attention part 3, the output Z = AV.

Then the attention matrix (8, 8) is multiplied by the Value matrix (8, 768), which gives the attention output (8, 768). In this output, each token’s row now holds information from the other tokens. As Figure 13 writes out for row 4, the [MASK] token's new vector z_4 is a weighted sum of all eight value rows, with the weights from Figure 12. Most of it comes from its own row and its two neighbors, "Bidirectional" and "Representation", which is the context it needs to predict the missing word. This combined information then moves on through the rest of the layer.

The following code implements Equation 6. The optional mask is a padding mask, not a causal mask, so every token can still attend to every other token in the sequence.

import math
import torch.nn.functional as F

class Attention(nn.Module):
    """softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V  (Equation 6)."""
    def forward(self, query, key, value, mask=None, dropout=None):
        scores = torch.matmul(query, key.transpose(-2, -1)) \
                 / math.sqrt(query.size(-1))                     # S, (..., n, n)
        if mask is not None:                                     # padding mask, never causal
            scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9)
        p_attn = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)                       # A, every row sums to 1
        if dropout is not None:
            p_attn = dropout(p_attn)
        return torch.matmul(p_attn, value), p_attn               # Z = A V, and A
6. Multi-Head Attention

Self-attention captures the relationships between words. Then why do we need multi-head attention? Self-attention captures the relationships between words from one perspective (it may capture the order of the sequence, grammatical structure, context, or dependencies between words). Multi-head attention captures the relationships between words from several perspectives at once, with the help of learned weights (parameters). Self-attention above works at the model dimension, while multi-head attention works at each head’s dimension.

Equation 10: Multi-head attention. Source: Attention Is All You Need paper.

The Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V) all come from the same input, the input embeddings or the output of the previous encoder layer.

BERT Base’s model dimension is 768, and the multi-head attention layer has 12 heads. To calculate the dimension of each head, we divide 768 by 12, which gives 64.

For each of these 12 heads, we need three components: the query, key, and value matrices. This means there are 12 separate attention mechanisms in the multi-head attention layer, and each one captures a different perspective of the input sequence.

These query, key, and value matrices are created with weight matrices. As shown in Equation 10 and illustrated in Figures 14 and 15, to create the query matrices, we multiply the input by 12 query weight matrices, each of size (768, 64). In practice this is organized a little differently, as explained in the code section. This gives 12 query matrices, one for each head, each of size (8, 64). Here, 64 is the dimension of the head, and 8 is the number of tokens in our example. The same process is repeated to create the key and value matrices for all heads. Each of these weight matrices is a linear layer.

Equation 11: The linear layer as computed by torch.nn.Linear.Figure 14: A linear layer as matrices, nn.Linear(768, 3072).
Important note to understand the linear layer: PyTorch stores the weight matrix as (current layer’s number of neurons, previous layer’s or input layer’s number of neurons), that is, output size × input size. We initialize the layer with the input size and the output size, nn.Linear(input vector size, output vector size). For example, the FFN of BERT Base has 768 input units and 3072 neurons in its hidden layer, so nn.Linear(768, 3072) holds a weight matrix W of size (3072, 768). The input vectors are multiplied by this matrix, transposed, which gives new vectors, and then the bias vector is added. This is a linear transformation of vectors: they move from one dimension (768) to another (3072), or to the same dimension.

Equation 11 is the linear layer operation in PyTorch. As emphasized in my previous articles, when it comes to linear layers or neural networks, it is essential to think in terms of matrices and vectors rather than neurons. In Figure 14, the input row x (768 numbers) is multiplied by Wᵀ, 768 rows of 3072. Column 2 of Wᵀ, which is row 2 of the stored W, dotted with x, plus the bias b_2, gives the output coordinate y_2, and each of the 3072 outputs is one such dot product. When x has 8 rows instead of one, the same bias row is added to every row of the result, which is called broadcasting.

Equation 12: Per-head projections in BERT Base.Figure 15: Query, key and value projections for each head.

The top of Figure 15 is head 1’s query with all its indices. X is 8 × 768, W₁^Q is 768 × 64, and Q₁ is 8 × 64: each token keeps its row, but the row is now 64 numbers. The bottom half shows all 36 projections at once, 12 heads for each of query, key and value, with every weight 768 × 64 = 49,152 numbers and every output 8 × 64.

Figure 16: Multi-head notation: 12 heads, each with its own Q, K and V of 8 × 64

Figure 16 lays out the result per head. Each head holds its own Q_h, K_h and V_h, all 8 × 64. Every head sees all 8 tokens but only its own 64 coordinates, and 12 × 64 = 768 brings the heads back to the model dimension.

Within each head, the same self-attention operation from Section 5 takes place, using that head’s query, key, and value matrices. Taking the first head as an example, the Q₁ matrix (8, 64) is multiplied by the transposed K₁ matrix (64, 8), resulting in an 8 × 8 matrix.

Next, this matrix is divided by the square root of the key’s dimension, which is 8 (since the key’s dimension is 64). The softmax is applied to each row, and the result is multiplied by the value matrix V₁, producing the attention output for head 1, with a size of (8, 64).

Equation 13: Attention inside one head.Figure 17: Attention inside each head. The attention maps are example patterns.

This same operation is repeated for all 12 heads, generating 12 attention head outputs, each of size (8, 64). Figure 17 shows why several heads help, with example attention maps. One head may learn to look one token back, another one token ahead, and another lets the [MASK] row gather from "Bidirectional", "Representation" and "Transformer" on both sides. Each head can learn its own pattern because each has its own weights, and studies of trained BERT models have found heads that specialize in this way.

Figure 18: Concatenating the 12 heads, then the output projection W^O.

Finally, the outputs from all the heads are concatenated, resulting in a single output of size (8, 768). In Figure 18, head 1 fills columns 0–63, head 2 columns 64–127, and head 12 columns 704–767. The concatenated output is linearly projected with a weight matrix W^O of size (768, 768), giving the multi-head attention layer output of size (8, 768). Concatenation only places the heads side by side. W^O is the step that mixes them, so every coordinate of the output can draw on every head.

The PyTorch implementation follows the same mathematics, with one difference in how the weights are organized, shown in Figure 19.

Figure 19: How the code computes all 12 heads with one projection and a reshape.

Instead of 12 separate 768 × 64 matrices, the code keeps one 768 × 768 matrix per role, with the 12 head matrices side by side. One product X W^Q gives an 8 × 768 Q whose columns 0–63 are exactly Q₁, columns 64–127 are Q₂, and so on. .view(B, n, 12, 64) splits each token's 768 numbers into 12 groups of 64, and .transpose(1, 2) moves the head axis in front of the tokens, giving one 8 × 64 matrix per head. Both ways give the same queries and the same number of parameters, but the fused version is one large matrix product instead of twelve small ones. The following code snippet will give you a better understanding of how MHA works in practice.

class MultiHeadedAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, h=12, d_model=768, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % h == 0      # 768 / 12 = 64, so the heads tile d_model exactly
        self.d_k = d_model // h      # head dimension, 64
        self.h = h                   # number of heads, 12
        # W^Q, W^K, W^V: each one nn.Linear(768, 768) = 12 heads of (768, 64) side by side
        self.linear_layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(d_model, d_model) for _ in range(3)])
        self.output_linear = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)     # W^O, (768, 768)
        self.attention = Attention()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

def forward(self, query, key, value, mask=None):         # each (B, n, 768), all X in BERT
        batch_size = query.size(0)                           # B, the batch size
        """
        The theory (Figure 15) uses 12 separate (768, 64) weight matrices per role.
        In practice one nn.Linear(768, 768) holds all 12 side by side (Figure 19).
        One matrix product gives (B, n, 768), .view splits the 768 columns into
        12 heads of 64, and .transpose moves the head axis in front of the tokens.
        Same outputs and the same parameter count, in one matrix product.
        """
        # 1) project, then split: (B, n, 768) -> (B, n, 12, 64) -> (B, 12, n, 64)
        query, key, value = [l(x).view(batch_size, -1, self.h, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
                             for l, x in zip(self.linear_layers, (query, key, value))]
        # 2) attention in all 12 heads at once: (B, 12, n, 64)
        x, attn = self.attention(query, key, value, mask=mask, dropout=self.dropout)
        # 3) concat: (B, 12, n, 64) -> (B, n, 12, 64) -> (B, n, 768)
        x = x.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(batch_size, -1, self.h * self.d_k)
        return self.output_linear(x)                         # W^O, (B, n, 768)

One more step comes before the feed-forward network: the Add & Norm block that follows attention in Figure 3.

Equation 14: Add & Norm, and LayerNorm.Figure 20: Add & Norm after multi-head attention, with LayerNorm on one row.

The attention output is added to the layer’s own input, which is the residual connection, and the sum is normalized. LayerNorm works on each token’s row by itself, as Figure 20 shows for row 4. It computes the mean μ₄ and the variance σ₄² of the row’s 768 numbers, subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, and then scales and shifts the result with γ and β, two learned 768-vectors shared by every token. BERT applies the normalization after the addition (post-norm), the arrangement used in the original Transformer. The same block follows the feed-forward network.

7. Feed Forward Network

In its simplest form, a feed-forward network is a type of neural network that consists of three layers: an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer. The number of input units in the input layer and the number of neurons in the output layer equal the model’s dimension (768). In the case of BERT, the hidden layer is four times (3072) the model’s dimension.

The FFN (Feed Forward Network) has a different role from attention. The attention mechanism gathers information from across the sequence. The attention layer captures the semantic and syntactic relationships between words and builds a contextual understanding of the sequence. The Feed Forward Network then processes that gathered information for each token on its own. It holds most of the model’s parameters, more than half of BERT Base (Figure 27), and it learns the patterns of the language humans use to communicate. By learning them, the model can predict the tokens.

Equation 15: The feed-forward network of BERT Base.Figure 21: The feed-forward network of BERT Base drawn as neurons.

The output from the multi-head attention layer, after Add & Norm, has a size of (8, 768) and is fed into the input layer of the Feed-Forward Network (FFN). Think of the input layer as a bridge that simply passes on the information without performing any operation.

Figure 21 shows the network as neurons, for one token. Each of the 3072 hidden units is connected to all 768 inputs, which is a 3072 × 768 weight matrix, and each of the 768 outputs is connected to all 3072 hidden units, a 768 × 3072 matrix. That is 2.36 million parameters on each side.

Figure 22: The feed-forward network on one token. Numbers are coordinate indices

Figure 22 shows the same token as matrices. Row 2 of W₁ dotted with x, plus the bias, then passed through GELU, gives the hidden coordinate h₂, and all 3072 rows together give h. W₂ takes h back to a 768-vector y. The hidden layer is four times wider than the token, which gives the nonlinearity room to work.

For the whole sequence, the input (8, 768) is multiplied by the transpose of the FFN hidden-layer weight matrix, which is stored with a size of (3072, 768), resulting in a matrix of size (8, 3072). Next, a bias vector (1, 3072) is added to each row of the resulting matrix, a process known as broadcasting. GELU applied to this matrix gives the hidden layer output.

Figure 23: FFN hidden layer and output layer operations on the whole sequence.

The output from the hidden layer (8, 3072) is then multiplied by the transpose of the FFN output-layer weight matrix, stored with a size of (768, 3072), resulting in a matrix of size (8, 768). Finally, an output-layer bias vector (1, 768) is added to each row, completing the FFN layer output. Both halves are shown in Figure 23. Every token passes through the same weights, independently of the others, which is why the “Attention Is All You Need” paper calls it position-wise. After Add & Norm, this output is passed on to the next encoder layer, or to the MLM head after the last layer. The bias vectors give every unit a learned offset, so a neuron can still be active when its weighted input adds up to zero.

In BERT, the GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) activation function is used. GELU weights each input by the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is smaller than it, x·Φ(x), which makes it a smooth version of ReLU. It can be approximated with the tanh formula in Equation 16, or more simply as GELU ≈ x·sigmoid(1.702x).

Equation 16: GELU and its two approximations.Figure 24: GELU, its tanh and sigmoid approximations, and ReLU.

In Figure 24, GELU is almost the identity for large positive inputs and almost 0 for large negative inputs, like ReLU. In between, it bends smoothly and dips slightly below zero, to −0.170 at x = −0.75, so small negative inputs still pass a little signal and a gradient. The tanh form, which the original BERT code uses, stays within 0.0005 of the exact curve. The sigmoid form is simpler and stays within about 0.02.

The following code implements the FFN and one encoder layer. With both halves in place, one encoder layer is attention and the FFN, each wrapped in Add & Norm, and BERT Base stacks 12 of them.

class PositionwiseFeedForward(nn.Module):
    # d_model is the model dimension (768), d_ff the hidden size (3072)
    def __init__(self, d_model=768, d_ff=3072):
        super().__init__()
        self.w_1 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff)      # W_1: weight (3072, 768), bias (3072)
        self.w_2 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model)      # W_2: weight (768, 3072), bias (768)
        self.activation = nn.GELU()              # x * Phi(x), Equation 16


def forward(self, x):                        # (B, n, 768)
        return self.w_2(self.activation(self.w_1(x)))   # (B, n, 3072) -> (B, n, 768)

class EncoderLayer(nn.Module):
    """Post-norm, as in BERT: X' = LN(X + MHA(X)),  X'' = LN(X' + FFN(X'))."""
    def __init__(self, d_model=768, h=12, d_ff=3072, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.attention = MultiHeadedAttention(h, d_model, dropout)
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model, eps=1e-12)
        self.ffn = PositionwiseFeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model, eps=1e-12)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
    def forward(self, x, mask=None):                                        # (B, n, 768)
        x = self.norm1(x + self.dropout(self.attention(x, x, x, mask)))     # Add & Norm 1
        return self.norm2(x + self.dropout(self.ffn(x)))                    # Add & Norm 2
8. Linear Layer and Softmax in MLM

After all the encoder layers (12), the final matrix (8, 768) is fed into the MLM head to predict the exact token for the Masked Language Model (MLM) task. The head has two parts: a transform, which is a 768 × 768 dense layer with GELU and LayerNorm, and then the output linear layer, whose weight is the word-embedding matrix itself, transposed.

Equation 17: The MLM head.Figure 25: The output layer of the MLM head, tied to the word embeddings.

Figure 25 shows the output layer as neurons. Each of the 30,522 outputs is connected to all 768 inputs, so its weight matrix is 768 × 30,522, the same size as the word-embedding table. BERT does not learn a second table. It reuses E_word (weight tying) and adds only a bias of 30,522 numbers, so the vector that represents a word at the input is also the one its output score is measured against.

Figure 26: The MLM head, from the last hidden state to the predicted token and the loss. Example probabilities

In Figure 26, the (8, 768) matrix is first transformed, row by row, into H̃. H̃ is then multiplied by E_wordᵀ (768, 30,522), and the bias is added. This results in a new matrix with a size of (8, 30,522), where 30,522 is the total number of tokens in the vocabulary. This resulting matrix is called the logits matrix. All 8 rows pass through the head here, as in the Hugging Face implementation, and only row 4 is used in the loss.

Next, the softmax function is applied to the logits matrix, which assigns a probability to every vocabulary token, row by row. The index with the highest probability score is selected as the output token.

When the masked token’s vector (in this case, the 5th token, index 4) passes through the head, it produces a logit vector of size (1, 30,522). This vector is then fed into the softmax function, which generates probability scores across all 30,522 possible tokens.

In our example, the correct output is the token “Encoder”, so the probability in its column should be high for the model to output “Encoder”: 0.62 in the example values of Figure 26. This means the model is confident that the correct output is “Encoder”. (In the real vocabulary, “encoder” is three WordPiece tokens, en, ##code and ##r, and each of those masked positions would get its own row and its own prediction.)

The loss is computed on the same row. The target is a one-hot row, all zeros except a one at the target index. Cross-entropy against it picks out the log-probability of the correct token, as Equation 18 shows. It is computed only at the masked positions, here row 4, and its gradient is what trains every weight in the model for the task.

Equation 18: Prediction and cross-entropy loss at the masked position.

The following code implements the MLM head. The output layer’s weight is assigned the word-embedding table, so the input embeddings and the output layer share the same (30522, 768) parameters.

class MaskedLanguageModel(nn.Module):
    # hidden --> model dimension (768), vocab_size --> 30522
    def __init__(self, word_embeddings, hidden=768):
        super().__init__()
        self.transform = nn.Linear(hidden, hidden)          # W_t, (768, 768)
        self.activation = nn.GELU()
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden, eps=1e-12)
        vocab_size = word_embeddings.num_embeddings
        self.decoder = nn.Linear(hidden, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.decoder.weight = word_embeddings.weight        # tied: the same (30522, 768) table
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(vocab_size))   # the only new output parameters
        self.softmax = nn.LogSoftmax(dim=-1)

def forward(self, x):                                   # (B, n, 768)
        x = self.norm(self.activation(self.transform(x)))
        return self.softmax(self.decoder(x) + self.bias)    # log-probs, (B, n, 30522)

The last block puts every piece from this article together and runs the eight-token example. With the weights of Hugging Face’s BertForMaskedLM copied in, its log-probabilities agree to within 3 × 10⁻⁶, and the parameter counts are identical.

class BERT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=30522, d_model=768, n_layers=12, h=12, d_ff=3072):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = BertEmbeddings(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([EncoderLayer(d_model, h, d_ff) for _ in range(n_layers)])
        self.mlm = MaskedLanguageModel(self.embeddings.word, d_model)

def forward(self, input_ids, mask=None):
        x = self.embeddings(input_ids)                      # (B, n, 768)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, mask)                              # (B, n, 768), 12 times
        return self.mlm(x)                                  # (B, n, 30522)

model = BERT().eval()
ids = torch.randint(1000, 30522, (1, 8))     # any 8 token ids
ids[0, 4] = 103                              # [MASK] at position 4, as in the figures
log_p = model(ids)
print(log_p.shape)                                   # torch.Size([1, 8, 30522])
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))    # 109514298
Figure 27: Where BERT Base’s 109.48 million parameters live.

Figure 27 counts the parameters by component. The 12 feed-forward networks hold just over half of BERT Base, the 12 attention layers about a quarter, and the word-embedding table a fifth. Positions, segments, and all the LayerNorms together come to under half a percent.

Important note: The weight matrices, bias vectors, LayerNorm parameters, position embeddings, and word embeddings are all learnable. They get updated during the backpropagation process while the model is being trained.
Conclusion

Some topics were not covered in this article, such as segment embeddings, the next-sentence prediction task, and fine-tuning BERT for specific tasks. However, it covers the most essential topics for a solid understanding of the BERT architecture: word and position embeddings, the masked language model task, self-attention and multi-head attention, the feed-forward network, and the linear and softmax layers of the MLM head.

By understanding the architecture, you can modify the loss function and the BERT architecture to suit your specific use case, and tailor BERT to your needs.

items.title: SaaSpocalypse Reality Check: Vendors Keep the Seat and Add a Meter
items.summary: Gartner said on July 1 that agentic systems deliver outcomes directly and make software invisible, which “breaks the link between user growth and revenue growth for many enterprise software vendors.” It estimated that up to $234 billion of enterprise application spending is exposed to what it calls agentic arbitrage between now and 2030. Yet Slack, Fin (formerly Intercom), Zendesk and Salesforce all still sell seats, and each has attached a meter to its AI. Software stocks sold off hard around the launch. Reuters, in a report carried by The Globe and Mail, said the S&P 500 software and services index had slid nearly 13% over five straight sessions and sat 26% below its October peak, and it named the plugin launch as one trigger for Tuesday’s selloff. ABC News reported that Thomson Reuters and LegalZoom each fell more than 15% on Tuesday, February 3. Not every analyst accepted the logic. JPMorgan’s Mark Murphy called it an illogical leap to extrapolate from the plugins to every company writing and maintaining bespoke software. The label stuck anyway. Gartner has since reframed it, calling the disaggregation of the legacy SaaS market “less an apocalypse and more of a metamorphosis.” Forecasts Point One Way, Earnings Another IDC’s FutureScape 2026, published October 23, 2025, predicts that by 2028 “pure seat-based pricing will be obsolete,” forcing 70% of vendors to refactor their value proposition into new models. Gartner’s $234 billion works out to roughly 20% of enterprise application SaaS spending by 2030. Both are forecasts, and IDC’s word is “pure”: a vendor that adds a meter to its seats is not what that prediction describes. The latest reported results show growth at seat-era vendors. Workday’s fiscal second-quarter subscription revenue rose 13.9% to $2.471 billion. Gartner’s July 27 forecast has worldwide software spending reaching $1.468 trillion in 2026, up 15.5%. Neither figure isolates seat counts, so neither proves or disproves compression. What they do show is that software budgets are still growing, which leaves the live question as how that money gets billed and which vendor collects it. The Seat Becomes the Floor Vendors are stacking a usage or outcome price on top of the per-user price instead of replacing it. Vendor Seat price Meter Slack Business+ at 15peruserpermonth,billedannually(18 monthly) Slackbot capped at 15 messages per member per week on Business+, with Flex Credits for usage beyond the cap Fin (formerly Intercom) Advanced helpdesk at $85 per seat per month Fin AI Agent from $0.99 per outcome, also sold with no seats alongside another vendor’s helpdesk Zendesk Suite Professional at $115 per agent per month, billed yearly Automated resolutions at $1.50 on a commitment or $2.00 pay as you go, beyond those included with each seat Salesforce Agentforce User License at $5 per user per month Requires Flex Credits, at $0.10 per action List prices as published on each vendor’s pricing page. Slack’s June 2025 repackaging shows the pattern in one move. Business+ rose from $12.50 to $15 per user per month on annual billing, the standalone AI add-on stopped being sold, and search, recaps, translations, file summaries and workflow automation moved into Business+ and the new Enterprise+ plan. Slack’s help center states that the plan price stays the same if a customer turns every AI feature off. Salesforce sells both models at once. Its Agentforce add-on costs $125 per user per month with unmetered employee usage, while the $5 license meters usage through Flex Credits. Marc Benioff told analysts on the August 26 earnings call that some customers still buy by user and by agent, others want consumption pricing, and some want to pay by outcome, according to a published transcript. Workday’s Gerrit Kazmaier said on the company’s August 27 call that because agent activity runs through Flex Credits, Workday monetizes every action regardless of the path a customer takes. One reading is that vendors are hedging: the seat keeps revenue predictable while the meter captures work that agents do beyond what a human user would. Read the table with one caveat. Slack is a Salesforce product, and Salesforce announced on June 15 that it signed a definitive agreement to acquire Fin, formerly Intercom, for about $3.6 billion, with closing expected in the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027. Three of the four rows sit inside one company or are about to. Zendesk, Workday and HubSpot sit outside it, and each also meters its agents by resolution, credit or outcome. Whoever Defines the Outcome Sets the Price Outcome pricing sounds simple until the units differ. Fin charges per outcome, Zendesk per automated resolution, HubSpot per resolved conversation and Salesforce per action. HubSpot’s Breeze Customer Agent moved on April 14, 2026, from $1.00 per conversation to $0.50 per resolved conversation. A resolution, a conversation and an action are different units, so $0.99, $0.50 and $0.10 cannot be compared directly. The definitions carry the real weight. Fin counts a resolution when the customer confirms the issue is resolved or does not ask for more help after Fin answers, and it bills one outcome per conversation. Default escalations, such as a customer asking for a human, are not billed, although a Procedure configured to end in a handoff to a human can be. Salesforce added its $0.10-per-action option in May 2025 alongside the $2-per-conversation price that its pricing page still lists for customer-facing agents. The implication is that procurement teams are about to negotiate definitions of a billable event more than they negotiate a price. Access Terms Are Part of the Price A seat prices a human login. An agent needs API access, and the vendor writes those terms. Since May 29, 2025, new installations of commercially distributed apps outside the Slack Marketplace face limits of one request per minute and 15 messages per request on Slack’s conversations.history and conversations.replies methods. Marketplace apps saw no rate-limit change, and internal customer-built apps are not affected. Slack’s developer changelog says the limits aim to prevent bulk data exfiltration by unvetted apps. Slack’s API terms, effective October 10, 2025, also bar using API data to train a large language model and bulk exporting Slack message and file data except under an additional agreement. A buyer who wants a third-party agent to work with Slack data now has to check which side of those lines the agent’s vendor sits on. Gartner and IDC both forecast agents taking over work that employees now do inside software. The contracts on offer today describe a hybrid in which seats set the floor and meters add whatever comes on top. The implication for the next renewal is concrete: get a written definition of every billable event, a cap on consumption charges, and the seat price with the AI features switched off.

items.summary_html:
The developer-to-production pipeline for Snowflake’s Cortex Agent GA enhancements — Personal Database sandboxes, temporary agents, COPY GRANTS, and the cost math on Cortex Search suspension.

Part 2 of 2 — Part 1: Your Cortex Agent Specification Is Visible to Every Role That Can Invoke It

From Personal Database to Production: Building Secure, Governed & Cost-Efficient Cortex Agents

Part 1 covered why secure agents exist and how spec redaction actually works — including the ownership gotcha that silently breaks redaction when ACCOUNTADMIN owns the agent. This article covers the production deployment pipeline: how to develop, validate, deploy, and operate a secure Cortex Agent with proper RBAC, zero-downtime updates, and cost controls.

The running example is the same release notes intelligence agent from Part 1.

The Developer Workflow: Personal Database to ProductionDevelop in Personal Database

Each developer creates agents in their own Personal Database. No CREATE AGENT privilege on shared schemas required.

CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT "USER$JSMITH".PUBLIC.release_notes_dev
  COMMENT = 'Dev iteration — testing new orchestration instructions'
  FROM SPECIFICATION $$
models:
  orchestration: claude-sonnet-4-6
instructions:
  response: "Testing revised response format — include release date in bold."
  orchestration: "Always use ReleaseAnalyst first, fall back to ReleaseSearch."
tools:
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_analyst_text_to_sql"
      name: "ReleaseAnalyst"
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_search"
      name: "ReleaseSearch"
tool_resources:
  ReleaseAnalyst:
    semantic_view: "release_intel_db.data.release_notes_model"
  ReleaseSearch:
    search_service: "release_intel_db.data.release_search"
    max_results: 5
$$;

The Personal Database agent references production data sources (the semantic view and search service) but lives in an isolated schema. No naming conflicts. No shared-schema privilege requirements.

Validate with Temporary Agent

Before promoting to production, create a temporary agent. Session-scoped — it disappears when the session ends and doesn’t require CREATE AGENT on the target schema.

CREATE TEMPORARY AGENT release_notes_validation
  FROM SPECIFICATION $$
models:
  orchestration: claude-sonnet-4-6
orchestration:
  budget:
    seconds: 30
    tokens: 16000
instructions:
  response: "Testing revised response format — include release date in bold."
  orchestration: "Always use ReleaseAnalyst first, fall back to ReleaseSearch."
tools:
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_analyst_text_to_sql"
      name: "ReleaseAnalyst"
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_search"
      name: "ReleaseSearch"
tool_resources:
  ReleaseAnalyst:
    semantic_view: "release_intel_db.data.release_notes_model"
  ReleaseSearch:
    search_service: "release_intel_db.data.release_search"
    max_results: 5
$$;

-- Validate
SELECT SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.DATA_AGENT_RUN(
    'release_notes_validation',
    $${"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "What features reached GA on September 16, 2026?"}]}]}$$
);

Temporary agent limitations: no versioning (COMMIT, aliases), cannot convert to permanent, and DATA_AGENT_RUN requires a fully qualified name for permanent agents (temp agents use the session namespace).

Promote with COPY GRANTS

The production agent already has grants to release_agent_consumer and analyst_role. COPY GRANTS preserves all of them during the replacement.

USE ROLE release_agent_owner;

CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE AGENT release_intel_db.agents.release_notes_agent
  COMMENT = 'Production release notes agent — v2, revised orchestration.'
  PROFILE = '{"display_name": "Release Intel", "avatar": "release-notes.png", "color": "blue"}'
  COPY GRANTS
  FROM SPECIFICATION $$
models:
  orchestration: claude-sonnet-4-6
orchestration:
  capabilities:
    analytical_search: true
  tool_not_accessible: accept
  budget:
    seconds: 30
    tokens: 16000
instructions:
  response: >
    You are a release notes intelligence assistant. Include the release
    date in bold for every feature mentioned. Be precise about GA vs
    Preview status.
  orchestration: >
    Always use ReleaseAnalyst first. Fall back to ReleaseSearch only when
    ReleaseAnalyst cannot answer.
tools:
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_analyst_text_to_sql"
      name: "ReleaseAnalyst"
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_search"
      name: "ReleaseSearch"
tool_resources:
  ReleaseAnalyst:
    semantic_view: "release_intel_db.data.release_notes_model"
    execution_environment:
      type: "warehouse"
      warehouse: "COMPUTE_WH"
  ReleaseSearch:
    search_service: "release_intel_db.data.release_search"
    max_results: 5
$$;

-- Verify grants survived
SHOW GRANTS ON AGENT release_intel_db.agents.release_notes_agent;

The operation is atomic. Consumers experience no interruption. Note: COPY GRANTS must come after PROFILE and before FROM SPECIFICATION — the clause ordering matters.

RBAC Design
-- Owner role: full specification access, deployment authority
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS release_agent_owner;
GRANT CREATE AGENT ON SCHEMA release_intel_db.agents TO ROLE release_agent_owner;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE release_intel_db TO ROLE release_agent_owner;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA release_intel_db.agents TO ROLE release_agent_owner;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA release_intel_db.data TO ROLE release_agent_owner;

-- Consumer role: invocation only, no spec visibility
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS release_agent_consumer;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE release_intel_db TO ROLE release_agent_consumer;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA release_intel_db.agents TO ROLE release_agent_consumer;
GRANT USAGE ON AGENT release_intel_db.agents.release_notes_agent
    TO ROLE release_agent_consumer;
-- Transfer ownership away from ACCOUNTADMIN (see Part 1)
GRANT OWNERSHIP ON AGENT release_intel_db.agents.release_notes_agent
    TO ROLE release_agent_owner REVOKE CURRENT GRANTS;
GRANT USAGE ON AGENT release_intel_db.agents.release_notes_agent
    TO ROLE release_agent_consumer;
Three roles, four capabilities, one asymmetry: everyone can invoke, few can read.

The consumer role has exactly 4 grants: USAGE on database, schema, agent, and warehouse. Zero grants on the DATA schema. Zero SELECT on any table. Zero GRANT_OPTION anywhere.

Graceful Degradation: What Happens When a Tool Goes Down

With tool_not_accessible: accept, the agent continues when a configured tool is unavailable. Here is what we observed with the Cortex Search service suspended:

Three query shapes, three routing paths — only one ever needs a retry.

The failover was genuinely graceful. Structured queries were unaffected. Conceptual queries took ~11 seconds longer (retry loop) but returned correct answers via SQL fallback.

The three tool_not_accessible values:

Three settings, two real policies: availability or compliance.Cost Optimization

The deployment has three cost levers:

The Cortex Search service was the largest controllable cost. With TARGET_LAG = '1 hour', it refreshes hourly regardless of data changes. For a dataset that updates weekly, that's waste.

-- Suspend to stop refresh costs
ALTER CORTEX SEARCH SERVICE release_intel_db.data.release_search SUSPEND;

-- Resume when needed (rebuilds from checkpoint)
ALTER CORTEX SEARCH SERVICE release_intel_db.data.release_search RESUME;

Break-even analysis: The search service costs ~0.04 credits/day. Each agent invocation costs ~0.0034 credits. At fewer than 12 conceptual queries per day, the search service costs more than the queries it serves. Recommended suspend threshold: fewer than 5 conceptual queries/day.

Both settings scale together: low volume suspends, high volume refreshes hourly.Trade-OffsWhen to Use Secure Agents
  • The specification contains proprietary orchestration logic
  • The agent is shared with external accounts or through Native Apps
  • Multiple teams have USAGE but should not see tool configurations
When to Avoid
  • Internal agents where all consumers are trusted
  • Development environments where spec transparency aids debugging
What to Monitor
-- Invocation volume and errors
SELECT execution_status, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE query_text ILIKE '%DATA_AGENT_RUN%release_notes_agent%'
    AND start_time > DATEADD('day', -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1;

-- Ownership hasn't reverted after replacement
SHOW AGENTS LIKE 'release_notes_agent' IN SCHEMA release_intel_db.agents;
-- Check: is_secure = true, owner = RELEASE_AGENT_OWNER (not ACCOUNTADMIN)
Key Takeaway
  1. The deployment pipeline is now complete. Personal Database → temporary agent → secure production agent with COPY GRANTS. Before September 2026, each step had friction.
  2. COPY GRANTS is the most operationally important enhancement. Losing grants during CREATE OR REPLACE was the most common production incident. COPY GRANTS makes agent updates as safe as view replacements. Clause order matters: COMMENT → PROFILE → COPY GRANTS → FROM SPECIFICATION.
  3. The semantic view is a zero-cost asset. Unlike the search service, it has no ongoing compute cost. The Cortex Analyst tool generates SQL at invocation time against metadata. This makes it the most cost-efficient component in the agent architecture.
  4. Suspend the search service when it costs more than the queries it serves. Below ~12 conceptual queries/day, the hourly refresh cycle is waste. The agent degrades gracefully to SQL-based search via tool_not_accessible: accept.

The gap between “agent prototype” and “production agent” just closed. Cortex Agents now have the same lifecycle primitives — secure objects, session-scoped testing, grant preservation, personal development sandboxes — that Snowflake’s mature object types have had for years.

items.title: Anthropic Reports User to the Police
items.summary: With mounting pressure on AI labs to curb the many real-world harms their products cause consumers, it’s never been clearer that they’re monitoring users’ conversations. Just ask Carli Michelle Heller, a woman arrested in Bonita Springs, Florida after allegedly telling Anthropic’s chatbot Claude about her plan to “shoot up” a nearby sheriff’s office. According to WINK News , Heller was charged with making a written threat of violence — a second-degree felony in Florida — after Anthropic’s internal monitoring software flagged her chat logs for human review. After being viewed by a human employee at Anthropic, WINK reports, the company determined that Heller’s plans rose to the level of a credible threat, ultimately informing local police. As Lee County Sheriff Carmine Marceno told local reporters in a statement, the woman admitted to using Claude like a “diary,” apparently unaware that her chat history could be read by Anthropic employees. There’s a genuine tension between user privacy and the responsibility of AI companies to try to head off violent events. In the aftermath of the February mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, for instance, it quickly emerged that the perpetrator had relied heavily on ChatGPT to plan her shooting. Not only had OpenAI staffers known about those chat logs prior to the shooting — they had been flagged for human review months prior — but company executives even tried to hide and later downplay their product’s role in encouraging the deadly attack. While Anthropic’s own track record on real-world harm is wretched, it seems the company is at least trying to avoid the same kind of incident — though with near-endless chatbot options now on the market, it could already be too late to prevent the next AI-assisted tragedy. items.title: Elon Musk is a trillionaire again
items.summary: Elon Musk is once again a trillionaire, a title he first held briefly in June after the SpaceX IPO. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Elon Musk has regained his trillionaire status thanks to a boost in SpaceX's stock price. Musk became the world's first trillionaire after the SpaceX IPO, but the stock price later fell. The stock price has rebounded, along with Musk's net worth. Elon Musk has regained his title as the world's only trillionaire. The Tesla CEO made history earlier this year by becoming the first person worth 13 figures after SpaceX's blockbuster initial public offering in June. Musk's wealth came back down a little closer to Earth after SpaceX's stock price fell following an initial surge. The rocket and AI company's stock price has been creeping back up since early August, reaching $171.09 as of Monday's market close. The nearly 8% boost on Monday brought Musk's net worth back over the trillion-dollar threshold, according to Forbes, which estimated his wealth at $1.046 trillion. Musk's wealth previously peaked on June 16 at $1.32 trillion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. While Musk had long been counted among the richest people in the world, the SpaceX IPO put him in another stratosphere. The second- and third-wealthiest people in the world as of Monday were Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Google cofounder Larry Page, worth $371 billion and $284 billion, respectively, according to Forbes. Much of Musk's net worth comes from stakes in SpaceX and Tesla, so it is typically tied to the success of those companies. SpaceX's stock reached its highest level since June on Monday. items.title: Why OpenAI's Regulatory Nightmare Is Only Getting Started
items.summary: Imagine working in the OpenAI department responsible for dealing with politicians and regulators right now—things must be so intense you could almost be working for Elon Musk . Every politician worth their salt, in countries around the world, is jumping into the AI safety fray. Case in point: On Monday, the New York City Council, that bastion of AI expertise, held a hearing to discuss the risks that AI poses to humanity. The council called whistleblowers like former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon to testify, along with officials from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta Platforms (Musk’s SpaceX didn’t show, and you can’t blame them). OpenAI is also facing a U.S. Senate investigation spearheaded by Sen. Josh Hawley, not to mention a Federal Trade Commission inquiry and another one by the Australian government. The state of Florida has gone to court to make life miserable for OpenAI. The Europeans, of course, have gotten into the act with their own inquiry. And these are just the regulators!
